claim: In a letter to Steve Jobs, Sean Connery refused to appear in an apple commercial.
justification: The fact-check could not verify or refute the claim that Sean Connery refused to appear in an Apple commercial via a letter to Steve Jobs, as the Record contains no Q&A, no retrieved evidence, and no consultedsources. Without reliable information — such as news articles, biographies, or interviews confirming whether Connery was ever approached, wrote such a letter, or what its content was — the claim cannot be evaluated, resulting in a verdict of **not enough information**.
gt_justification: The answer and sources show that the claim was published in a fake news site so the claim is refuted.

claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
justification: The fact-check confirms that leaked Trump Administration documents from late October 2020, part of a $250 million HHS COVID-19 advertising campaign overseen by Assistant Secretary Michael Caputo, did indeed reference singer-songwriter Billie Eilish and contained the exact characterization that she was "destroying our country and everything we care about." The [Washington Post](https://money.yahoo.com/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html) first reported on the documents, which were treated as authentic by Democratic lawmakers who cited them in a letter to HHS Secretary Alex Azar, and the story was widely covered by outlets like [NME](https://www.nme.com/news/music/trump-admin-says-billie-eilish-is-destroying-our-country-and-everything-we-care-about-2803852) and [Just Jared](https://www.justjared.com/2020/10/29/trump-administration-official-accused-billie-eilish-of-destroying-our-country/). While the document was likely quoting Eilish's own remarks from the Democratic National Convention, the leaked material presented this characterization in a way that media interpreted as the administration's assessment, and Eilish was ultimately excluded from the campaign for being deemed "not a Trump supporter." The administration did not officially comment on the documents' authenticity, but the core assertion—that leaked Trump Administration documents contained this characterization of Eilish—is well-supported by multiple credible sources.
gt_justification: Seems that the Wzshington post accused the singer wrong lyrics. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.
justification: The claim's assertion that French visa cancellations and deportations of Pakistani citizens were **"due to" Imran Khan's criticism of Macron** is entirely unsupported by evidence. While Macron did make controversial comments about Islam in October 2020 ([India Today](https://www.indiatoday.in/world/story/backlash-over-french-president-emmanuel-macron-comment-on-islam-explained-boycottfrenchproducts-1735400-2020-10-27)) and Khan did publicly criticize those remarks ([MM News](https://mmnews.tv/pm-imran-lashes-out-at-french-president-macron-for-anti-muslim-attitude/)), and the Pakistani Consulate in France did publish a tweet on October 31, 2020 about visa cancellations ([archived tweet](https://web.archive.org/web/20210629013122/https://twitter.com/PakConsulateFr/status/1322495811993903104)), the French government never issued any official statement confirming, explaining, or justifying these actions. The Consulate itself acknowledged that "no clarification has yet [been] provided by the French immigration department regarding the visa cancellation of our citizens," and no source establishes a causal link between Khan's criticism and the French immigration actions. The specific numbers (183 and 118) also could not be fully verified from the archived content. Attributing the visa cancellations to Khan's criticism presents a partial situation in a way that fabricates a causal connection with no supporting evidence.
gt_justification: The tweet was not the official government page and there is no evidence that visas were cancelled so the claim is refuted.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
justification: The claim that "UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world" is false and fabricated. There is no credible evidence in UNESCO's official records, press releases, resolutions, or publications—neither in 2020 nor any other year—identifying the Nadar community or any other group as "the most ancient race in the world" ([ssn.edu.in](https://www.ssn.edu.in/history//created)). UNESCO's institutional mandate is fundamentally opposed to such classifications; its landmark 1950 *Statement on Race* and subsequent revisions explicitly rejected racial hierarchies and the notion of ranking human groups by "ancientness," affirming instead that all humans belong to a single species with a common origin ([openlearning.unesco.org](https://openlearning.unesco.org//created), [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/11/181108142340.htm/created)). UNESCO's actual declarations pertain to World Heritage Sites, Intangible Cultural Heritage, and cultural diversity—not racial classifications of communities ([icomos.org](https://www.icomos.org/images/DOCUMENTS/Charters/GA2011_Declaration_de_Paris_EN_20120109.pdf)). The Nadar community is historically documented as a Tamil caste from southern India (Tamil Nadu and Kerala), traditionally associated with toddy-tapping and palmyra cultivation, whose origins are uncertain and not substantiated by any legitimate scholarly basis for the "most ancient race" designation ([familytreedna.com](https://www.familytreedna.com/groups/nadar/about/background)). The claim has been widely debunked by fact-checkers, and the sources promoting it are unreliable or fabricated.
gt_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.

claim: Republican Matt Gaetz was part of a company that had to pay 75 million in hospice fraud. They stole from dying people.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Matt Gaetz is a Republican ([Mother Jones](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2019/07/how-matt-gaetz-used-daddys-money-to-become-trumps-favorite-congressman/)) and was affiliated with Vitas Healthcare Corporation as a "co-owner and executive board member" ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/matt-gaetz-tweets-cryptic-warning-to-michael-cohen-ahead-of-hearing//created)), which paid a $75 million civil settlement for defrauding Medicare through false hospice claims ([DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/chemed-corp-and-vitas-hospice-services-agree-pay-75-million-resolve-false-claims-act)). However, an important nuance emerged: the DOJ source clarifies the fraud involved "submitting false claims for hospice services to Medicare" for patients "who were not terminally ill," meaning the money was effectively stolen from Medicare (a federal program) by fraudulently enrolling non-terminal patients, rather than being taken directly from dying people as the claim suggests. Additionally, Gaetz was not personally named, charged, or held liable in the case—the settlement was paid by the company. While the characterization "they stole from dying people" is a slight oversimplification of the actual victims (Medicare and non-terminal patients), the core factual elements of the claim—Gaetz's Republican affiliation, his role with the company, the $75 million payment, and the hospice fraud nature—are supported by the evidence.
gt_justification: The company was sold in 2004 and the law suit was filed in 2013

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
justification: The fact-check found insufficient evidence to confirm or refute the claim that the US and Western allies systematically used their media outlets to publish fabricated information about Chemical Weapons Convention non-compliance. While some sources reference leaked documents and whistleblowers alleging a "coordinated US-led campaign" related to chemical weapons allegations (see [Atlantic Council publication](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Breaking-Ghouta_English.pdf/created)) and claims that outlets like the BBC were "fed false intelligence," several cited URLs do not match their referenced content (e.g., a [Nevada system administration page](https://nshe.nevada.edu/system-administration/compliance//created) cited for BBC claims, a [Libya chronology page](https://www.armscontrol.org/factsheets/LibyaChronology/created) cited for OPCW findings), raising serious questions about source veracity. Furthermore, the OPCW itself has rejected allegations that its reporting on Syrian chemical weapons was falsified, and the authenticity of the leaked documents remains contested. Given that the claim originates from SANA—a source with a clear interest in the narrative—and that the gathered evidence lacks verified primary sources confirming direct government coordination with media to publish fabricated information, the fact-check concludes there is not enough information to reach a definitive verdict.
gt_justification: Refuted by answer/source.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
justification: The fact-check found that the claim's central assertion of 160,000 preventable COVID-19 deaths is supported by the [Columbia University NCDP study](https://ncdp.columbia.edu/custom-content/uploads/2020/10/Avoidable-COVID-19-Deaths-US-NCDP.pdf), which estimated between 130,000 and 210,000 avoidable deaths by comparing U.S. per-capita mortality rates with those of comparable high-income nations (South Korea, Japan, Australia, Germany, Canada, and France) under a counterfactual scenario of more timely and coordinated public health responses. Biden's "160,000" figure falls squarely within that published range. The claim's other assertion—that more than 225,000 people had died by October 30, 2020—is slightly inflated, as [CDC data](https://www.un.org/en/desa/149-million-excess-deaths-associated-covid-19-pandemic-2020-and-2021/created) shows the cumulative confirmed death toll on that date was 218,373, though the figure is approximately in the right ballpark. Overall, the core substantive policy claim is well-grounded in peer-reviewed research, leading to a verdict of **supported**.
gt_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
justification: Joe Biden's criticism of Donald Trump over his minimal federal income tax payments during the 2020 campaign is well-documented, with [The New York Times report (as covered by CBC)](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/trump-taxes-fake-news-1.5741186) revealing that Trump paid no federal income taxes in 10 of the 15 years prior to 2017, originally reported as $750 for 2016/2017 and [later corrected to $0](https://apnews.com/article/d2960cf56ff447ba48f2e1c0da435d84), making the substance of Biden's claim even more accurate than the $750 figure he cited. Trump's statement about being "smart" and "gaming the system" in reference to taxes is corroborated by a [House transcript](https://docs.house.gov/meetings/FA/FA00/20190410/109306/HHRG-116-FA00-Transcript-20190410.pdf) from a 2016 debate context, confirming the core elements of the claim align with the documented facts.
gt_justification: True, question mark required (?)

claim: You’re watching the cheaters and all those people that send in the phony ballots. … They want to have the count weeks after November 3.
justification: The claim is refuted by overwhelming evidence from multiple credible sources. Historical mail-in ballot fraud rates are extremely low, with a DOJ investigation finding only 0.00000013% of ballots were fraudulent in 2002-2004 elections, according to a [Brennan Center analysis](https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/analysis/Briefing_Memo_Debunking_Voter_Fraud_Myth.pdf). Courts—including Trump-appointed judges—consistently rejected fraud claims, with a [Washington Post analysis via Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/alisondurkee/2020/10/23/trump-mail-in-voter-fraud-claims-have-no-merit-courts-rule-new-jersey/) finding that out of 90 voting cases decided, not one judge backed Trump's claim that fraud was significant enough to sway a presidential election, with judges describing the allegations as "highly speculative," "conjectural," and even "a fiction." The only specific "evidence" Trump cited—50,000 erroneous ballots in Ohio—was actually a [scanner malfunction that caused ballots to be incorrectly sent out](https://www.bbc.com/news/54562611), not fraudulent ballots being submitted. The extended counting period Trump complained about was the result of established, legal state-level procedures, including a [Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/20/supreme-court-will-allow-pennsylvania-to-count-ballots-received-up-to-3-days-after-the-election.html) upheld by a 4-4 U.S. Supreme Court vote allowing ballots postmarked by Election Day to be received until November 6, with 18 states having post-Election Day deadlines—half of which Trump won in 2016—confirming these were bipartisan legal procedures rather than evidence of fraud.
gt_justification: The mail in ballots have to be counted no later than 7 days after election day. so that it would be weeks later is refuted.

claim: You see the number today? 33.1 GDP. The biggest in the history of our country by almost triple, right? Almost triple. Now it’s very much bigger than any GDP we’ve ever had. You have to go back to the 1950s, and then it’s less than half. This is the greatest number, 33.1 percent.
justification: The claim that the U.S. GDP grew at 33.1%—the "biggest in the history of our country"—is factually accurate: the Commerce Department reported a record annualized quarterly GDP growth rate of 33.1% for Q3 2020, the highest since quarterly data began being tracked in 1947, surpassing the previous record of 3.9% set in Q1 1950 ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/gdp-q3-growth-33-1-percent/), [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2020/10/29/us-economy-turns-in-record-q3-growth-but-crisis-is-not-over), [USAFacts](https://usafacts.org/articles/gdp-grew-74-third-quarter-2020-remains-lower-it-was-pre-pandemic-levels/)). However, the claim cherry-picks by omitting critical context: the 33.1% figure is an annualized projection (the actual quarter-over-quarter growth was 7.4%), and it represented a rebound from an unprecedented 31.4% annualized contraction in Q2 2020 caused by COVID-19 lockdowns ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/29/economy/gdp-report-trump-biggest-best-factcheck/index.html)). Furthermore, Trump's characterization that 33.1% was "almost triple" the previous record is a significant understatement—33.1% is actually more than eight times larger than the prior record of 3.9% ([USAFacts](https://usafacts.org/articles/gdp-grew-74-third-quarter-2020-remains-lower-it-was-pre-pandemic-levels/)). By presenting the rebound figure without the preceding collapse, using the annualized rather than the actual quarterly rate, and understating the magnitude of the record, the claim creates a misleadingly triumphant impression of the state of the economy.
gt_justification: There is only one question and that is unanswerable. There is no evidence about the GDP in 2020 when the claim was made. Therefore there is not enough evidence to refute or support the claim.

claim: Donald Trump, when he thinks of climate change, he says hoax. Well, guess what? Speaking of hoaxes, remember what he said about these increasing violent hurricanes and the frequency? He actually said, maybe we should detonate a nuclear bomb over the Atlantic. By the way, the same stable genius who said the biggest problem we had in the Revolutionary War is we didn’t have enough airports.
justification: The evidence consistently supports each of the three substantive assertions and the character reference in the claim. Trump did repeatedly characterize climate change as a "hoax," including in a [2012 tweet](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-says-climate-change-not-a-hoax-but-not-sure-of-its-source), before partially walking it back in 2018. He did suggest [dropping a nuclear bomb "inside the eye of the hurricane"](https://www.businessinsider.in/trump-has-reportedly-suggested-using-nuclear-bombs-to-stop-hurricanes-from-striking-the-us-a-move-that-scientists-have-called-wacky-and-agree-wont-work/articleshow/70834740.cms) as it moves across the Atlantic, a proposal raised on multiple occasions during official White House briefings and documented in a 2017 NSC memo. He did make the [Revolutionary War airports gaffe](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/trump-revolutionary-war-airports/) during his July 4, 2019 "Salute to America" speech, saying troops "took over the airports." And he has repeatedly [referred to himself as a "stable genius"](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2019/07/11/trump-again-calls-himself-stable-genius/1703154001/) since first using the term in January 2018. The comedic paraphrase of the airports remark accurately captures its substance. Verdict: **supported**.
gt_justification: There is a few too many claims in this claim, so while one is true, he did say we should detonate a nuclear bomb, i cannot confirm all are true

claim: The U.S. surgeon general and the Centers for Disease Control both previously said that ‘masks are not effective in preventing [the] general public from catching coronavirus.’
justification: The claim is misleading in its attribution: the specific quoted phrase—"masks are not effective in preventing [the] general public from catching coronavirus"—is a near-verbatim reproduction of [U.S. Surgeon General Jerome Adams's February 29, 2020 tweet](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/04/02/coronavirus-us-surgeon-general-asks-cdc-to-see-if-face-masks-are-effective.html), not a CDC statement. While the CDC did hold a substantively aligned position in early 2020—[a spokesperson stating that "CDC does not recommend that people who are well wear a facemask to protect themselves from respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19"](https://www.vox.com/2020/3/31/21198132/coronavirus-covid-face-masks-n95-respirator-ppe-shortage)—the agency expressed this in different words, and Adams himself [confirmed in an April 3, 2020 press briefing](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/surgeon-general-against-masks/) that both his office and the CDC "originally recommended against the general public wearing masks" because it "was not deemed" to have a "significant impact" on whether a healthy person would contract COVID-19. By early April 2020, [both reversed their guidance](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/coronavirus-surgeon-general-jerome-adams-wearing-masks-face-the-nation/) as evidence emerged about asymptomatic transmission. The claim is therefore substantively accurate but presents a Surgeon General quote as if both he and the CDC said the same thing verbatim, constituting a misleading attribution.
gt_justification: There is a 79% reduction made in certain situations. But not effective in certain other situations.

claim: New Zealand’s new Food Bill bans gardening
justification: The claim that New Zealand's new Food Bill bans gardening is demonstrably false. New Zealand's actual food legislation is the **Food Act 2014**, which was passed on 27 May 2014 and came into effect on 1 March 2016 (see [Wikipedia: Food Act 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_Act_2014)), not introduced in October 2020. The Act regulates commercial food safety and trade but contains no provisions prohibiting personal gardening or home cultivation. Multiple reputable news organizations, including [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/), [The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/), [Huffington Post](https://www.huffpost.com/), and [BuzzFeed](https://www.buzzfeed.com/), have covered and debunked this assertion as a hoax or internet myth ([Know Your Meme](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/new-zealand-gardening-law-hoax)). The false claim appears to have originated from mischaracterizations in low-credibility sources such as a [UPU postal prohibitions list](https://www.upu.int/UPU/media/upu/files/postalSolutions/programmesAndServices/postalSupplyChain/customs/prohibitedArticles/ListOfProhibitedArticles.pdf) and [accesstolaw.com](https://www.accesstolaw.com/commonwealth/new-zealand/nzlii/), and the claim itself even appears in an [ICFJ guide on fake news and disinformation](https://www.icfj.org/sites/default/files/2018-07/A%20Short%20Guide%20to%20History%20of%20Fake%20News%20and%20Disinformation_ICFJ%20Final.pdf), further confirming its status as misinformation. No specific legislative text, section, or clause supporting a gardening ban has been identified in any authoritative source.
gt_justification: The bill is not into legislation for now. I see claim as false.

claim: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
justification: The claim is refuted because the scientific evidence consistently shows that face masks **reduce** but do not **stop** the spread of COVID-19. The WHO Director-General explicitly stated that "[m]asks alone will not protect you from COVID-19," a pre-October 2020 systematic review found only modest reductions in transmission (~6% in community settings, ~19% in households), and a laboratory study by Kim et al. concluded that even fully sealed N95 masks "were not able to completely block the transmission of virus droplets/aerosols" ([Kim et al., 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33087517/); [systematic review](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.01.20049528v1)). The epidemiological literature uniformly uses language of "reducing risk" rather than complete prevention—a meta-analysis reported an odds ratio of 0.38 (a ~62% reduction), not elimination ([PubMed PMID 33347937](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33347937/)). The claim's absolute language overstates the evidence. Additionally, the attribution is questionable: Yinon Weiss's article titled "These 12 Graphs Show Mask Mandates Do Nothing to Stop COVID" appears to refute rather than assert this position, suggesting the claim may have been misattributed or extracted as a straw-man argument from the [original Federalist article](https://thefederalist.com/2020/10/29/these-12-graphs-show-mask-mandates-do-nothing-to-stop-covid/).
gt_justification: From the question and answer pair it does indeed seem that face masks are useful in stopping the spread of covid19. Therefore, the claim is supported.

claim: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) in Pakistan/India was removed from the United Nations (UN) list of “unresolved disputes”.
justification: The fact-check could not be completed because the Record contains no documented investigation, no Q&A, and no retrieved evidence to evaluate the Claim that Jammu and Kashmir was removed from the UN list of "unresolved disputes." Without any supporting or refuting evidence — such as official UN statements, Security Council resolutions, or verification of the archived source ([archive.ph/3oBfZ](https://archive.ph/3oBfZ)) — there is no factual basis to determine whether the Claim is true, false, or partially true. The verdict remains **not enough information**.
gt_justification: The answer and source show that they were never on the list so the claim is refuted.

claim: Illegal drug, border crossings, and human smuggling activities have decreased in areas where barriers are deployed in the United States.
justification: The claim is partially supportedby [DHS data](https://www.dhs.gov/news/2020/10/29/border-wall-system-deployed-effective-and-disrupting-criminals-and-smugglers) showing significant apprehension decreases in specific barrier sectors (e.g., 87% in FY20 vs. FY19 in areas with new border wall system, 79% in RGV Zone 1, and 60–81% in El Paso zones), but it cherry-picks this data by omitting the critical confounding factor that [Title 42 expulsions](https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/stats/cbp-enforcement-statistics/title-8-and-title-42-statistics-fy2021) were implemented on March 21, 2020—seven months before the claim—which would independently cause dramatic decreases in border crossings regardless of barriers. The claim also extends to "illegal drug" and "human smuggling" activities, yet the available evidence primarily documents apprehension/crossing decreases, not drug trafficking or human smuggling specifically, and a [1995 GAO report](https://www.gao.gov/assets/ggd-95-30.pdf) found that decreases in barrier sectors were offset by increases in non-barrier sectors due to displacement effects, contradicting the implied narrative of overall reduction. Furthermore, [GAO reported in 2017](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/homesec/R45888.pdf) that CBP had not developed systematic metrics to assess border fencing's contribution to its mission, leaving the claim's specific causal attribution unsubstantiated.
gt_justification:
15 miles of new barriers seems unlikely to account for the halving of illegal crossing from 2019 to 2020. Particularly as 2019 is the outlier in the period 2018 to 2020.

However the claim isn't about causation, only the fact that numbers have decreased in these areas. The 2018-2020 figures are for the whole border so it's impossible to assess if this trend is true in areas with barriers (which make up around half of the land border).

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
justification: The claim that "plentiful evidence" shows masks do not meaningfully help against aerosol transmission of COVID-19 is refuted by the available evidence. At the time of the claim (October 2020), the [WHO and CDC](https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/covid19/universal-masking-statement-04232020.pdf/created) characterized the evidence on aerosol transmission as "insufficient" rather than concluding masks were ineffective, and they actively recommended masks. Peer-reviewed [NIST laboratory research](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2020/06/face-coverings-made-layered-cotton-fabric-likely-slow-spread-covid-19) demonstrated that certain multi-layered cotton fabrics could block a meaningful percentage of particles in the SARS-CoV-2 size range (~110 nm), and N95 respirators are specifically engineered to filter ≥95% of airborne particles. Real-world epidemiological studies, including [Lyu & Wehby (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32543923/), found mask mandates were associated with significant declines in COVID-19 growth rates, estimating over 200,000 cases were averted by May 2020. No major scientific institution had concluded masks were ineffective against aerosol transmission. The claim also improperly generalizes across mask types without acknowledging the critical distinction between cloth, surgical, and N95 respirators. The claim's author, Yinon Weiss, has a background in [military and business](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yweiss), with no credentials in epidemiology, virology, or public health. The assertion of "plentiful evidence" demonstrating mask ineffectiveness is contradicted by laboratory data, real-world studies, and the positions of major health organizations.
gt_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
justification: Eric Holder's claim that "all USA ballots arriving after Election Day will be thrown out" is false and constitutes cherry-picking. U.S. election administration is decentralized, with each state setting its own rules, and numerous states—including California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Washington—explicitly allowed mail-in/absentee ballots postmarked on or before Election Day to be received and counted days or even weeks afterward, as documented by [FiveThirtyEight](https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/why-were-planning-for-an-election-day-that-could-last-months/), [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/pictures/how-to-vote-by-mail-in-every-state-and-u-s-territory/), and the [Chicago Board of Elections](https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/vote-mail). The U.S. Supreme Court reinforced this variability by issuing a 4-4 decision allowing Pennsylvania to count ballots received up to three days after Election Day ([NACo](https://www.naco.org/articles/supreme-court-allows-pennsylvania-count-ballots-three-days-after-election-day)). While it is true that many states required ballots to be received by Election Day, Holder's sweeping, unqualified assertion omits these significant state-level exceptions, presenting a partial truth as if it applied universally to all ballots across all states.
gt_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
justification: The claim is a **cherry-picking** distortion. While it is technically true for states using a strict "received by Election Day" deadline—such as [Wisconsin](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/supreme-court-won-t-let-late-mail-ballots-count-wisconsin-n1244865) and Michigan—several other states, including [Pennsylvania](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2020/10/19/supreme-court-allows-penn-count-ballots-received-up-nov-6/5899677002/), [California](https://www.democracydocket.com/analysis/mailing-in-your-vote-important-dates/), and Maryland, used "postmarked by" deadlines that explicitly allowed ballots postmarked on or before Election Day to be counted even if they arrived days or weeks afterward (e.g., Pennsylvania accepted ballots up to 3 days after, California up to 17 days). The U.S. Supreme Court even issued a 4-4 ruling in October 2020 that left Pennsylvania's extended receipt deadline intact. By omitting this critical state-by-state variation, the claim falsely implies that *all* such ballots nationwide would be discarded, which was demonstrably not the case.
gt_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.

claim: Video shows attack of French embassy in Sudan
justification: The video does not show an attack on the French embassy in Sudan; it is actually footage from the **September 14, 2012 attacks** on the **British and German embassies** in Khartoum, which were part of broader anti-film protests across the Muslim world, as documented by [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/20120914-britain-germany-sudan-embassies-targeted-protests-anti-islam-film-usa-egypt-libya). While a real attack on the French embassy in Khartoum did occur on October 28, 2020 (reported by [Al Jazeera, France24, Reuters, and AFP](https://www.britannica.com/event/1983-United-States-embassy-bombing/created)), the specific video being shared is old 2012 footage that was misattributed, a finding consistent with the [BoomLive fact-check](https://www.boomlive.in/fake-news/2012-embassy-attacks-in-sudan-falsely-shared-as-attack-on-french-embassy-10392) and confirmed via reverse video searches identifying it as the "2012 Sudan embassy attack video." The French embassy was not among the embassies targeted in the 2012 attacks, making the claim **refuted**.
gt_justification: It is the "German" embassy that was under attack in Sudan.

claim: Viral video purportedly shows Pakistani opposition MPs chanted ‘Modi, Modi’ (India's PM)  inside the Pakistani Parliament
justification: The most methodologically rigorous investigation, conducted by [facthunt.in](https://facthunt.in/posts/1484), cross-referenced the viral clip with the original, longer footage of the October 26, 2020 National Assembly session available on the Dunya News YouTube channel and corroborated its findings with a [Dawn newspaper](https://www.dawn.com/) report, concluding that the MPs were actually chanting "voting-voting" (demanding a vote during the chaotic session) rather than "Modi-Modi." This directly refutes the core assertion of the claim. While other sources, such as [The Wire](https://thewire.in/media/amit-malviya-bjp-fake-news/) and [NDTV](https://archives.ndtv.com/articles/2013-01.html), appeared to confirm the "Modi, Modi" interpretation, they largely restated the viral claim rather than independently verifying it against primary source footage, making the facthunt.in finding the more credible and evidence-based conclusion.
gt_justification: They were shouting voting not modi

claim: Taylor Zundel claimed on Instagram that she and other early voters in Utah, were unable to cast ballots in the 2020 presidential elections, as they were told they had already voted.
justification: The fact-check confirmed that Taylor Zundel did post an Instagram video around October 27, 2020, about an incident during early voting in Utah, but a key detail in her claim was misleading: according to the [archived Herman Cain article](https://web.archive.org/web/20201119224000/https://hermancain.com/instagram-testimony-people-showing-vote-already-voted/), it was her **husband** and at least one other voter who were told they had already voted — not Zundel herself, who merely witnessed the event. Additionally, no official evidence of voter fraud was found; the source, a politically conservative blog, characterized the situation as either "bureaucratic incompetence... or fraud" without confirming either, and there is no independent verification from official Utah election records or mainstream news outlets to substantiate the specific incident. The verdict is **cherry-picking** because the claim misleadingly implies Zundel was personally affected when she was only a witness.
gt_justification: She was able to vote, after a temporary problem.

claim: Trash Can Plastered With 'Ballot Box' Sign In Philadelphia Was Intended To Get People To Toss Their Ballots In The Trash.
justification: Multiple sources confirm that a trash can in Philadelphia was deliberately marked with a "Ballot Box" sign in October 2020 and placed near an official ballot drop box, as documented by the [Philadelphia city government voting website](https://vote.phila.gov/ballot-drop-off//created). Philadelphia election officials explicitly characterized the sign as "a deliberate attempt to mislead voters into discarding ballots," and [FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/10/in-pennsylvania-rallies-trump-distorts-voting-issues//created) reported the incident was referred to the District Attorney and election board for investigation. This official characterization directly aligns with the claim that the trash can sign was intended to get people to toss their ballots in the trash.
gt_justification: From the question and answer pair it seems that the claim is refuted.

claim: Joe Biden wants to ban fracking
justification: The claim that "Joe Biden wants to ban fracking" is based on cherry-picked statements from his 2019 and early 2020 Democratic primary debates—including a July 2019 remark about eliminating fossil fuels and a March 2020 comment about "no new fracking"—but it ignores substantial and critical context that significantly changes the picture. During the general election, Biden explicitly and repeatedly stated, "I am not banning fracking. Let me say that again. I am not banning fracking," as reported by [Energy Now](https://energynow.com/2020/09/the-biden-flip-flop-u-s-presidential-hopeful-biden-now-says-he-would-not-ban-fracking/) and [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/23/politics/biden-fracking-fact-check/index.html), and his actual 2020 campaign platform focused on measures like methane pollution limits and restrictions on new federal-land drilling rather than a complete ban. Furthermore, as [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-10-21/here-s-why-biden-couldn-t-ban-fracking-but-could-restrict-it) noted, a president lacks the legal authority to unilaterally ban fracking on private and state lands, making the claim not only selectively sourced—per [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/election-2020-joe-biden-donald-trump-pennsylvania-elections-c28fbf9d921915f3a65c01e6c4cebcf6)—but also misleading about both Biden's actual policy positions and presidential powers.
gt_justification: From the Q&A it seems Joe biden has never said he wants to ban fracking. So the claim is refuted.

claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
justification: No evidence, sources, or documentation were gathered during the fact-checking process to evaluate whether Germany's Foreign Minister Heiko Maas made the statement in question regarding Thailand's King Maha Vajiralongkorn. Without any retrieved material, credible news reports, official transcripts, or press statements, it is impossible to confirm or deny the Claim, resulting in a determination of "not enough information."

According to the QA pairs, Germany's Foreign Minister Heiko Maas stated that they are "watching what the Thai king gets up to in Germany" as "politics concerning Thailand should not be conducted from German soil". The Thai King is accused of conducting politics from Germany. However, the claim states that Maas said that the King "didn't do anything illegal" which is not proven to be true. Therefore, this claim is refuted.

claim: McDonald’s Azerbaijan's official account was promoting the military taking of Nagorno-Karabakh.
justification: The fact-check consistently refutes the claim across multiple sources, all of which explicitly state that McDonald's Azerbaijan never published any post about Nagorno-Karabakh on October 27, 2020, or any other date. Both McDonald's corporate and the Azerbaijan franchise confirmed that no such post promoting military action existed ([source](https://www.lee.k12.al.us/domain/739/created)), and no credible news outlet or fact-checker has verified the alleged post ([source](http://www.quirkandspoon.com/2015/09//created)). While some sources mention a "deleted" post ([source](https://www.yes-abroad.org//created)), others clarify that the verified McDonald's Azerbaijan account never posted about Nagorno-Karabakh at all ([source](https://www.globalissues.org/article/448/backing-up-globalization-with-military-might/created)). There is no documented public reaction from Armenian users, the Armenian Embassy, or Armenian-American organizations to a post that, according to all available evidence, never existed. The evidence actively contradicts the claim, with no supporting evidence found whatsoever.
gt_justification: Evidence is provided but question should really mention it is an instagram account.

claim: Ivermectin is a treatment for coronavirus.
justification: The fact-check record contains no documented evidence to evaluate the claim that "Ivermectin is a treatment for coronavirus." No fact-checking questions were posed, no searches were conducted, and no sources were consulted to determine the status of ivermectin as a COVID-19 treatment as of October 2020. Without any supporting or refuting evidence gathered in the record, there is insufficient information to reach a determination on the claim's accuracy.
gt_justification: Ivermectin is licensed for anti parasitic used but not enough evidence yet exists for treatment against coronavirus.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
justification: The claim that mosquito bed nets—both treated and untreated with insecticide—are ineffective and harmful is directly contradicted by robust scientific evidence. A landmark Gambian study showed that insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) reduced overall child mortality by approximately 63% and malaria-attributable mortality by 70% ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1675368](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1675368/)). A Cochrane Review found ITNs provided 17% protective efficacy against child mortality and reduced uncomplicated malaria incidence by 50% in stable malaria areas, while untreated nets also offer meaningful protection of roughly 30–50% ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15106149](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15106149/)). Although some sources raise concerns about pyrethroid safety, major health authorities such as the WHO, CDC, and UNICEF have extensively reviewed ITN safety and consider them safe for human use, with no robust documented evidence linking proper ITN use to cancer, asthma, or other chronic health conditions. The claim is therefore clearly refuted by both peer-reviewed research and the consensus of leading public health organizations.
gt_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact

claim: Pogba Has Quit The French National Team Over Macron's Remarks on Islam.
justification: The claim that Paul Pogba quit the French National Team over Emmanuel Macron's remarks on Islam is refuted by the most authoritative and direct evidence available. Paul Pogba himself publicly denied the retirement reports, and [the Mirror corrected its initial reporting](https://www.mirror.co.uk/sport/football/news/breaking-man-utd-star-paul-22904740) on the matter after Pogba labeled the claim as "fake news." Additionally, the claim originated from [Troll Football Nepal](https://www.facebook.com/OfficialTFN/photos/a.2080854138854114/2743164972623024/?type=3), a non-credible source, and while Macron did make controversial remarks about Islam in October 2020 (described as a religion "in crisis" and plans to combat "Islamist separatism," as [reported by Dawn](https://www.dawn.com/news/1583290)), this political backdrop does not validate the false claim about Pogba's retirement. The secondary sources mentioning a formal resignation — such as a [France24 tag page](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/religion/) and a [bank's terms-and-conditions page](https://www.federalbank.co.in/en/tandc/) — are low-credibility or irrelevant and do not override Pogba's own explicit denial.
gt_justification: Debunked by Pogba himself.

claim: The Wire called Durga puja racist and the goddess Durga a sex worker
justification: The claim that "The Wire called Durga puja racist and the goddess Durga a sex worker" misrepresents the outlet's actual reporting. According to [AltNews](https://www.altnews.in/the-wire-did-not-disrespect-durga-excerpt-from-2016-article-misrepresented/) and The Wire's founding editor Siddharth Varadarajan himself, the words "racist" and "sex worker" appeared within a **quotation of Union Minister Smriti Irani's February 2016 parliamentary speech**, in which she read out extracts she attributed to a JNU pamphlet — they were not The Wire's own editorial characterization of the festival or the goddess. The viral claim stripped away this quotation framing, making it appear that The Wire independently labeled Durga Puja and the goddess this way. While some third-party sources described the article as having "directly called Durga puja racist and the goddess a sex worker, without critical framing or attribution," these characterizations themselves misrepresented the original context, which was clearly a report on Irani's speech. Varadarajan's public clarification on Twitter confirmed the excerpt was being circulated by "Hindutva loonies" as if it were The Wire's own view, when it was actually a quoted parliamentary statement. Therefore, the claim is **refuted**.
gt_justification: The claim is refuted as the magazine The Wire was not calling the gods those things but it was from a pamphlet so the claim is refuted.

claim: Paul Pogba, who plays for Manchester United and the French national team, retired from international football in response to French President Macron’s comments on Islamist terrorism.
justification: The claim is fully supported by the evidence. Paul Pogba was associated with Manchester United as of October 2020 ([NDTV archives](https://archives.ndtv.com/articles/2018-03.html/created)) and represented the French national team, from which he announced his retirement on October 26, 2020, as reported by [L'Équipe via Gistmania](https://www.gistmania.com/talk/topic,476044.0.html/created) and [Eurosport](https://www.eurosport.com/football/premier-league/2015-2016/chelsea-transfer-news-chelsea-target-danny-rose_sto4845109/story.shtml/created). President Macron had made comments on October 21, 2020, declaring Islamism a threat to France and vowing action against "Islamist separatism" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Manchester_United_F.C._players/created)), and Pogba's representatives explicitly cited these remarks as the reason for his retirement, stating he could no longer represent a team whose leader stigmatized his religion ([Fox Sports Australia](https://www.foxsports.com.au/football/premier-league/rumour-mill/rumour-mill-jose-to-break-world-record-atletico-want-striker-back-french-duo-happy-to-stay-at-clubs/news-story/a17c6641531ccf58fed140d446a4161f/created), [Stretty News](https://strettynews.com/2020/10/26/pogba-quits-france-after-president-macrons-remarks-on-islam//created)). The five-day timeline between Macron's speech and Pogba's retirement is consistent across verified reports.
gt_justification: Denied by Pogba.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed as US Supreme Court Justice on October 26, 2020
justification: The claim that Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed as US Supreme Court Justice on October 26, 2020 is **supported**. Although the record contains no formally documented Q&A evidence or retrieved sources, the claim aligns with well-established historical fact: the US Senate confirmed Barrett on that date by a 52–48 vote, and she was sworn in the following day. Key sources that would typically corroborate this include [Senate roll-call records](https://www.senate.gov/), contemporaneous news reports, and the [Supreme Court's official biography](https://www.supremecourt.gov/).
gt_justification: Although the date is not confirmed in the QA pair, it is stated in the source for the Answer provided.

claim: The New York post Endorsed Donald trumps bid for re-election.
justification: The claim is refuted by multiple sources that consistently state the New York Post did not endorse Donald Trump for re-election in 2020 and that the cited article was fabricated. Ballotpedia notes that the editorial board "explicitly decided not to endorse any presidential candidate in 2020, breaking its tradition" of backing Republican nominees, while other sources characterize the archived article as a "hoax or manipulation." Although the claim origin URL points to a [web.archive.org snapshot](https://web.archive.org/web/20210119183455/https://nypost.com/2020/10/26/the-new-york-post-endorses-president-donald-j-trump-for-re-election/) with a purported endorsement title, the weight of evidence from [History.com](https://www.history.com/topics/us-presidents/donald-trump), [Statista](https://www.statista.com/statistics/229817/readers-of-the-new-york-post-ny-daily-edition), [The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2018/04/how-the-1970s-shaped-trumps-vision/557465/), and [Xinhua](http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2020-08/24/c_139314489.htm) converges on the finding that no such genuine endorsement was ever published.
gt_justification: Claim is correct

claim: America went from 75,000 flu deaths last year in 2019 to almost 0 in 2020
justification: The claim is refuted on multiple counts. The CDC estimated approximately 61,200 flu deaths for the 2018–2019 season ([Time](https://time.com/5610878/2018-2019-flu-season/)), not 75,000, and the 2017–2018 season was actually the deadliest recent one at around 80,000 deaths ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2018/09/26/health/flu-deaths-2017--2018-cdc-bn/index.html)). More critically, flu deaths in 2020 did not approach zero; the CDC estimated 24,000–62,000 deaths for the 2019–2020 season ([Contagion Live](https://www.contagionlive.com/view/how-deadly-was-the-2019-2020-flu-season)), and while COVID-19 mitigation measures did reduce flu activity in 2020–2021, no credible public health authority ever characterized U.S. flu deaths as "almost 0."
gt_justification: There were an estimated 21,909 flu deaths during the 2019-2020 flu season, not 75,000. The CDC graph does show flu levels at almost zero; however, that could be due to the year not being finished as of yet. The graph could always change as we enter the winter months, seeing as this claim was made in October. Hence, there is some conflicting evidence here.

claim: The United States, New Zealand, U.K., Australia, and the EU have not included the NDF in their official list of terrorist groups.
justification: The claim is partially supported but ultimately undermined by conflicting evidence. For the **United States**, **New Zealand**, and the **United Kingdom**, the NDF was not separately listed as a terrorist organization—only the CPP/NPA was designated, as confirmed by the [Vera Files fact-check](https://verafiles.org/articles/vera-files-fact-check-badoy-errs-claiming-ndf-tagged-terror), the [U.S. State Department's FTO list](https://2001-2009.state.gov/s/ct/rls/fs/08/103392.htm), and the [UK Home Office's Proscribed Organisations list](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/266038/List_of_Proscribed_organisations.pdf). For the **EU**, the January 2020 Council Decision (CFSP 2020/20) did not list the NDF, though the subsequent decision (CFSP 2020/1132) in effect by October 26, 2020 was not verified. However, the claim is directly contradicted regarding **Australia**: while the [Vera Files fact-check](https://verafiles.org/articles/vera-files-fact-check-badoy-errs-claiming-ndf-tagged-terror) states the CPP-NPA was listed "excluding NDFP," a [Philippine News Agency article](https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1105350) explicitly states "The CPP-NPA-NDF is listed as a terrorist organization by... Australia." This direct contradiction on Australia's designation, combined with the unverified status of the EU's updated terrorist list, renders the overall claim one supported by conflicting evidence.
gt_justification: NDF is not listed on any of the official lists of terrorist groups.

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
justification: The claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was pre-planned with Bill Gates' help is refuted by overwhelming evidence from multiple authoritative sources. A peer-reviewed study in *Nature Medicine* confirms SARS-CoV-2 originated through natural processes, ruling out laboratory manipulation or deliberate genetic engineering ([Scripps](https://www.scripps.edu/news-and-events/press-room/2020/20200317-andersen-covid-19-coronavirus.html)), and the U.S. Intelligence Community explicitly stated the virus was "not manmade or genetically modified" ([DNI](https://www.dni.gov/index.php/newsroom/press-releases/press-releases-2020/3447-intelligence-community-statement-on-origins-of-covid-19)). The Gates Foundation's documented actions were reactive—announcing $150 million in response funding in April 2020 after the pandemic emerged—not proactive planning ([Gates Foundation](https://www.gatesfoundation.org/ideas/media-center/press-releases/2020/04/gates-foundation-expands-commitment-to-covid-19-response-calls-for-international-collaboration)). While the Foundation co-sponsored Event 201, a October 2019 pandemic simulation, Johns Hopkins clarified it "did not make a prediction" about COVID-19 and the fictional scenario differed significantly from the actual outbreak ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/03/26/fact-check-bill-gates-backed-pandemic-exercise-didnt-predict-covid-19/5081854002/)). Bill Gates' pre-2020 statements addressed general pandemic preparedness, not any specific plan for COVID-19 ([GeekWire](https://www.geekwire.com/2020/bill-gates-warned-us-covid-19-like-pandemic-watch-ted-talk-2015/)). The claim conflates legitimate preparedness efforts with alleged involvement in engineering or pre-arranging the pandemic, and no credible government, intelligence agency, scientific journal, or court of law has ever concluded the pandemic was deliberately pre-planned.
gt_justification: It is clearly stated in the QA that the notion that covid is pre-planned is false, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
justification: The claim is **refuted**. Robin Vos did not lose his seat in the 2018 election—he won re-election in Assembly District 63, defeating Democrat Joel Jacobsen ([Madison.com](https://madison.com/robin-vos-timeline/article_ce58f640-24d2-5fdb-9c8f-ce3a3930ba88.html)). While Republicans did lose one seat in the Assembly in 2018, it was the 14th District seat vacated by Rep. Dale Kooyenga, who chose to run for State Senate rather than seek re-election, making it an open seat flip rather than a defeat of a sitting incumbent ([CBS58](https://www.cbs58.com/news/vos-emerges-as-wisconsin-republican-leader-as-walker-gets-ready-to-step-down)). [Ballotpedia](https://ballotpedia.org/Wisconsin_State_Assembly_elections,_2018) explicitly confirms that "no incumbents were defeated in the general election" in 2018. The claim fundamentally misrepresents what occurred by conflating Vos personally losing his seat with the broader Republican caucus losing a seat.
gt_justification: True

claim: Breitbart News reports that the daughter of Delaware Democratic Senator Chris Coons and seven other underage girls were featured on Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: The claim concerns what Breitbart News reported, not whether the underlying allegations are true. Evidence confirms that Breitbart did publish a report making these specific allegations, as documented in [Ground News](https://ground.news/article/d3c74388-e567-47f9-b709-c5721ccd1b10) and [PolitiFact](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0069841/created). Chris Coons is verified as a Democratic Senator from Delaware ([GoUpstate](https://www.goupstate.com/story/news/2010/11/03/coons-beats-odonnell-in-delaware-senate-race/29846150007/)), and he does have a daughter, Maggie Coons, who was publicly identified in connection with the allegation by Republican Senate candidate Lauren Witzke. While the underlying factual claims about the laptop's contents have been disputed and debunked by fact-checkers, and the laptop's contents have not been independently verified through forensic analysis ([Washington Examiner](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/fbi-and-doj-do-not-believe-hunter-biden-laptop-part-of-russian-disinformation-campaign)), the claim as literally stated about Breitbart's reporting is accurate.
gt_justification: There is no evidence of Breitbart news reporting on Hunter Biden so the claim is refuted.

claim: Hunter Biden, son of US President Joe Biden has died.
justification: The claim that Hunter Biden died is false. Hunter Biden is alive, having published his memoir "Beautiful Things" in 2021, married Melissa Cohen in 2019, and remained publicly active well beyond October 2020. The claim originated from a hoax post on 4chan dated October 25, 2020, and was explicitly debunked and labeled FALSE by [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/10/27/fact-check-rumors-hunter-biden-dead-4-chan-hoax/3754066001/), which also noted that Joe Biden continued normal campaign activities during that period—attending church on October 25 and campaigning in Pennsylvania and Georgia in the following days—behavior inconsistent with a family bereavement. Snopes similarly [fact-checked the claim](https://www.today.com/video/4chan-murder-photos-tracked-back-to-ip-address-355274819647?ex=rt&featureFlag=true/created) and flagged it as false misinformation tied to the 2020 election. No reliable news outlet, official government source, or family member confirmed his death, and no death certificate or obituary exists. Additionally, the claim inaccurately describes Joe Biden as "US President" when, on October 25, 2020, Donald Trump was still the sitting president; Biden did not take office until [January 20, 2021](https://www.history.com/topics/us-presidents/joe-biden).
gt_justification: The second answer shows that Hunter Biden is still alive and therefore the claim is refuted.

claim: 5G causes COVID-19.
justification: The claim that "5G causes COVID-19" is unequivocally refuted by the gathered evidence. COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus that originated through natural zoonotic spillover ([CIDRAP](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/scientists-exactly-zero-evidence-covid-19-came-lab)), not by electromagnetic radiation. While 5G is a form of radiofrequency electromagnetic radiation ([Medical News Today](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/326141)), viruses like SARS-CoV-2 require a biological host to replicate and are transmitted through respiratory droplets, aerosols, and surface contact—mechanisms that electromagnetic waves cannot facilitate. No legitimate peer-reviewed study has demonstrated a causal link between 5G exposure and COVID-19, and the World Health Organization explicitly considers such a link "biologically and physically impossible" ([VOA News](https://www.voanews.com/a/covid-19-pandemic_australia-parliament-debunks-5g-covid-19-conspiracy-theory/6189256.html)). Multiple authoritative bodies, including the WHO, an Australian parliamentary committee, and Australia's chief medical officer, have debunked this conspiracy theory, confirming there is no scientific basis for the claim.
gt_justification: The CDC and WHO said  you need to come into contact physically with the coronavirus to become infected by it, and as the EMFs from 5G cannot carry viruses, they cannot bring you into contact with the virus

claim: Rock musician Jon Bon Jovi performed for 12 people and 7 pumpkins at a campaign event for Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden in Pennsylvania.
justification: The claim contains partially accurate but highly misleading information. While Jon Bon Jovi did perform at a drive-in campaign event for Joe Biden in Pennsylvania's Luzerne County on October 24, 2020, credible sources such as the [Asbury Park Press](https://www.app.com/story/entertainment/music/2020/10/24/jon-bon-jovi-hitting-campaign-trail-big-i-vote-concert-support-biden/6022327002/) and [NBC Philadelphia](https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/politics/decision-2020/bon-jovi-plays-at-biden-event-after-candidate-visits-bucks-county/2572756/) confirm the event was a drive-in rally where "hundreds of cars honked their horns," indicating a significantly larger audience than the claim suggests. The specific "12 people" figure likely refers only to non-vehicle attendees standing near the stage, while the inclusion of "7 pumpkins" is not corroborated by any source and appears to be a fabricated or distorted detail. By omitting the crucial drive-in context, the claim creates a misleading impression of a sparsely attended event, warranting a **cherry-picking** verdict.
gt_justification: Claim states 12 people but QA pairs say 230 cars so if they only had the driver in them it would be a minimum of 230 people.

claim: Wearing face masks can cause infections from bacteria such as staphylococcus.
justification: The claim is rated as **cherry-picking** because it presents a theoretical and extremely rare risk as a meaningful health concern. While a theoretical mechanism exists—mask-induced skin irritation could create an opening for *Staphylococcus aureus* (which naturally colonizes the skin and nostrils of 20–80% of the human population, per a [Frontiers in Microbiology](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmicb.2018.02419) study) to enter the body—two dermatologists interviewed by [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/09/18/fact-check-staph-infections-common-not-caused-face-masks/5692064002/) (Dr. Zaineb Makhzoumi and Dr. Adam Friedman) explicitly confirmed that face masks do not cause staph infections, with Makhzoumi stating no association between mask use and staph infection has been observed. [Health Desk](https://health-desk.org/articles/is-there-any-evidence-for-a-relationship-between-staph-infections-and-using-masks-to-prevent-the-spread-of-covid-19) acknowledges this theoretical pathway but describes it as "very rare" and "highly unlikely to occur," requiring specific conditions such as pre-existing skin lesions, mask-induced chafing, or poor mask hygiene. No peer-reviewed scientific studies demonstrate a causal link between mask use and staphylococcus infections, and the claim omits this critical context, selectively highlighting the theoretical mechanism while ignoring the strong expert consensus and the rarity of the scenario.
gt_justification: Prolonged mask use can cause side effects such as acne, difficulty breathing, headaches, impaired cognition, rashes, and skin breakdown. It also interferes with vision, communication, and thermal balance. There isn't evidence it can cause staphylococcus. Staphylococcus is caused by a break in your skin, such as a cut, scrape, or burn, the bacteria can enter your body and cause an infection.

claim: An 'anti-Black Lives Matter' flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump during a Waukesha campaign rally.
justification: The fact-check record contains no evidence, sources, or results from any verification process—no questions were asked, no answers gathered, and no documentation consulted beyond the original claim posted by Jeff Sharlet on [Twitter](https://web.archive.org/web/20210529130838/https://twitter.com/JeffSharlet/status/1320189238214799360). Without visual or video evidence from the Waukesha campaign rally, credible news reports, or any corroborating or refuting sources, there is insufficient information to determine whether an "anti-Black Lives Matter" flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump. The verdict is therefore **not enough information**.
gt_justification: The 2nd QA seems to support this claim.

claim: Donald Trump said that $15 an hour is too much for essential workers
justification: The claim attributes a specific statement to Donald Trump about $15/hour being "too much for essential workers," but no documented evidence in the record confirms Trump used this exact framing. While Trump did oppose raising the federal minimum wage to $15/hour, his stated reasoning centered on the impact on small businesses and potential job losses—not on essential workers specifically. The claim therefore takes a true underlying position (Trump's opposition to a $15 federal minimum wage) and reframes it with the "essential workers" characterization that Trump himself did not use, creating a significantly different and more inflammatory impression. This constitutes a misleading characterization of Trump's actual statements, fitting the pattern of `cherry-picking`.
gt_justification: Even though Trump said similar to this, it was taking out of context. The claim was cherrypicking.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
justification: Professor Paul Lehner did publicly discuss "pox parties" at a [Science Media Centre press conference on October 23, 2020](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html), but the Claim cherry-picks his remarks by stripping away essential qualifying context. Lehner explicitly framed pox parties as a "last resort option in the absence of a vaccine" and added the speculative hedge "but we'll have to wait and see," making his actual position far more cautious and conditional than the Claim suggests. Furthermore, the broader scientific consensus at the time strongly opposed deliberate infection strategies: the [WHO called herd immunity through natural infection a "dangerous fallacy"](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/covid-19-herd-immunity-backed-white-house-dangerous-fallacy-scientists-n1243415), 80 scientists signed an open letter in *The Lancet* opposing it, and [multiple COVID-19 vaccines were already in late-stage Phase III trials](https://cepi.net/news_cepi/321-vaccine-candidates-against-covid-19-now-in-development/) with imminent authorization—making the deliberate infection of children an unnecessary and risky proposition that Lehner himself did not outright endorse.
gt_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.

claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.
justification: The fact-check could not be completed because the Record contains no evidence, sources, or prior Q&A results to evaluate the claim that cutting the umbilical cord immediately deliberately denies babies natural immunity to create a market for vaccines and medication. Without any retrieved medical or scientific evidence on cord-clamping practices or the motivations of medical professionals, a substantive determination cannot be made based on the documented fact-check work, resulting in a verdict of **not enough information**.
gt_justification: From the 2nd answer it is evident that the umbilical cord does not have anything to do with the babies getting vaccinated. The vaccination has to happen regardless, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
justification: The claim that the umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth is refuted by authoritative medical guidelines and peer-reviewed research. The [WHO recommends late cord clamping at approximately 1–3 minutes after birth](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK310522/), while [ACOG recommends delayed cord clamping for at least 30–60 seconds](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/ask-acog/what-is-delayed-cord-clamping)—not a full hour. Peer-reviewed research demonstrates that [placental transfusion typically plateaus at around 140 seconds (roughly 2–3 minutes)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4687772/), meaning the blood transfer is essentially complete within minutes, making a 1-hour delay medically unnecessary. The few sources (such as Cryo-Cell, a cord blood banking company with commercial interests) that claim a 1-hour delay are inconsistent with the actual published guidelines from WHO and ACOG, and no major peer-reviewed medical guideline recommends waiting a full 60 minutes before clamping the umbilical cord.
gt_justification: It seems the cord needs to be cut after a few minutes. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Joe Biden said he wants to ban fracking in the US.
justification: Joe Biden explicitly and repeatedly denied wanting to ban fracking in the United States, directly contradicting Charlie Kirk's claim. In the very ABC News town hall video cited as the source of the claim, Biden stated "I do not propose banning fracking" ([ABC News transcript](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/read-full-transcript-joe-bidens-abc-news-town/story?id=73643517)), and in a Pittsburgh speech he emphatically declared "I am not banning fracking. Let me say that again: I am not banning fracking" ([source](https://www.uagetinvolved.org/content/joe-biden-i-am-not-banning-fracking)). His 2020 campaign platform did not propose a complete ban—only an end to new fracking leases on federal land, which represents just 10% of all national leases ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/biden-says-fracking-jobs-wont-chopping-block-if-hes-elected-1516793)). While Biden made earlier primary debate remarks like "no new fracking" and "we would make sure it's eliminated" that his campaign clarified as referring to federal permits rather than a total ban ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/23/politics/biden-fracking-fact-check/index.html)), his general election position was unambiguously against banning fracking, and fact-checkers characterized claims to the contrary as "repeated false claims."
gt_justification: Biden has said he would ban fracking and has also said he would rule out banning fracking.

claim: 99% of people recover from COVID-19.
justification: The claim is rated as **cherry-picking** because, while it is technically defensible under the most favorable metric—the global infection fatality rate (IFR) of 0.15–0.20% ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33026101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33026101/)), which implies ~99.8% survival—it selectively ignores critical context that contradicts the impression of COVID-19 as benign. The WHO-reported case fatality rate was approximately 2.7% ([WHO Weekly Epidemiological Update, Oct 12, 2020](https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/situation-reports/20201012-weekly-epi-update-9.pdf)), mortality reached 7.8% in those over 80 ([BMJ](https://www.bmj.com/content/369/bmj.m1327)), and the claim omits the prevalence of long COVID and persistent post-acute complications affecting many "recovered" patients. Furthermore, Trump provided no supporting data for the figure ([statesman.com](https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/07/07/fact-check-are-99-of-coronavirus-cases-lsquototally-harmlessrsquo-as-trump-said/42604755/)), and fact-checkers such as PolitiFact rated similar "99% harmless" claims as false, noting that "nothing says that it's harmless for 99% of the people it touches." By presenting only the most favorable survival statistic while excluding higher fatality rates, age-related risks, and long-term complications, the claim creates a misleadingly benign picture of the disease.
gt_justification: Q&A 1 shows that the claimed  99% recovery rate around October 2020 was actually only  67.97% around October 2020 according to the Johns Hopkins University of Medicine

claim: The US saw the best carbon emission numbers in 35 years under President Donald Trump's administration.
justification: The claim is technically true in a narrow sense—US carbon emissions during Trump's term did reach lows not seen in roughly three decades (2019 being the lowest since 1992 per [Climate Change News](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2020/10/06/us-emissions-four-years-president-trump/), with further drops in 2020)—but it is misleading because it implies the Trump administration caused these reductions. In reality, emissions actually **rose by 3.4% in 2018** according to [Rhodium Group](https://rhg.com/research/preliminary-us-emissions-estimates-for-2018/), the Trump administration actively rolled back Obama-era climate regulations like the Clean Power Plan and methane rules rather than implementing new reduction policies ([Inside Climate News](https://insideclimatenews.org/news/25042017/donald-trump-climate-change-clean-power-plan-paris-agreement/)), the significant 2020 decline was driven by COVID-19 pandemic-related economic shutdowns ([C2ES](https://www.c2es.org/content/u-s-emissions/)), and the rate of decline during Trump's term (0.5% through 2019) was far slower than during Obama's eight years (11%). The underlying downward trends were driven by market forces—particularly the switch from coal to natural gas and renewables—and Obama-era policies, not by Trump administration actions, making this a classic case of cherry-picking favorable outcomes while ignoring contrary policy direction and actual causation.
gt_justification: It seems the emission was lowest under president Bush in 1991, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Twitter now putting warnings on tweets that are just unedited clips of Biden saying he would end fracking
justification: The claim is refuted because Twitter's October 2020 labeling policy explicitly targeted **manipulated or deceptively edited media**—not unedited clips of real statements—using a "three-pronged test" focused on whether content was synthetic/manipulated, shared deceptively, and likely to cause harm ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/04/twitter-unveils-new-rules-to-tackle-deepfakes-ahead-of-2020-election.html)). The specific incident around October 23, 2020, involved Twitter labeling a **deceptively edited "cheapfake"** video of Biden—cut to make it appear he said "we can only re-elect Donald Trump" when his actual full statement was different—not an unedited clip about fracking ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/social-media/facebook-twitter-put-warning-label-edited-video-biden-n1153506)). While Biden did make real statements about fracking on the campaign trail ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/video-resurfaces-kamala-harris-saying-she-wants-ban-fracking-after-saying-biden-will-not-during-1537304)), there is no evidence Twitter labeled any unedited clips of those statements, and Twitter's broader Civic Integrity Policy update targeted election misinformation rather than unedited political speech ([PopSugar](https://www.popsugar.com/news/twitter-integrity-policy-election-retweets-update-47868604/1000), [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/10/09/922028482/twitter-expands-warning-labels-to-slow-spread-of-election-misinformation)). The claim mischaracterizes both the nature of the labeled content (edited, not unedited) and the subject matter (not fracking).
gt_justification: Twitter put those warning on tweets about Biden's speech because they were misleading but the tags were not only on the Biden's tweet

claim: People who do not vote for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 elections will not get the COVID vaccine free of cost.
justification: The claim is refuted because no COVID-19 vaccine had been approved in India as of the claim date (October 22, 2020)—approvals did not come until January 2021 ([NIH source](https://www.nih.gov/sites/default/files/research-training/initiatives/covid-19-strategic-plan/coronavirus-strategic-plan-20200713.pdf/created))—making any denial of access impossible at that time. The Indian government's official vaccine distribution policy contained no conditions related to political affiliation; the Health Ministry promised universal procurement and distribution for all states ([The Hindu Business Line](https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/a-non-existent-covid-vaccine-gets-caught-in-a-political-storm/article32921495.ece)). While the BJP and its allies used free vaccine promises as election campaign rhetoric in 2020 state elections (notably Bihar and Tamil Nadu), these were political campaign promises, not official government policy, and the claim conflates campaign messaging with actual policy. Although one suspicious PIB source seemingly referenced BJP officials making such statements, its URL format raises credibility concerns, and no independent fact-checking organization confirmed the claim. The assertion that non-BJP voters would be denied a free COVID-19 vaccine is unsupported by any official policy and conflates political campaign messaging with government action.
gt_justification: The answer shows that the claim is false and so the claim is refuted.

claim: President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the WORLD BANK and International Monetary Fund.
justification: The claim is definitively refuted by overwhelming historical evidence. The World Bank and IMF were established at the [Bretton Woods Conference in 1944](https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/137956/WP14.pdf), in New Hampshire, USA, by 44 Allied nations, with the principal architects being [Harry Dexter White](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/international-bank-of-reconstruction-and-development.asp) (U.S. Treasury) and John Maynard Keynes (United Kingdom). Dr. Jose Rizal was [executed in 1896](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_Day)—nearly 50 years before these institutions existed—making it impossible for him to have founded them. Ferdinand Marcos, [born in 1917](https://www.amazon.com/prime-video/actor/Ferdinand-Marcos/amzn1.dv.gti.dd9c0d4c-9b1d-4b2b-abe2-174c75f7134e/), was only 27 years old and had not yet entered politics in 1944, and did not become President of the Philippines until 1965, more than two decades after these institutions were founded. Neither individual had any role in establishing the World Bank or IMF.
gt_justification: On the World Bank’s website and the IMF’s website, it states both entities were conceived and established in 1944, following the Bretton Woods agreement on a global economic framework post-World War II.

claim: The FBI is in possession of the president of the US's son  Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: The fact-check finds the claim's core assertion — that the FBI was in possession of Hunter Biden's laptop — to be supported. Multiple sources confirm the FBI obtained the laptop on December 9 or 19, 2019, through a [grand jury subpoena](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8866457/Laptop-allegedly-belonging-Hunter-Biden-linked-FBI-White-Collar-money-laundering-probe.html) issued to the Wilmington, Delaware repair shop owner, John Paul Mac Isaac, as part of a federal money laundering investigation. The laptop had been [dropped off at Mac Isaac's shop in April 2019](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/hunter-biden-emails-computer-repair-store-owner-john-paul-mac-isaac), and Mac Isaac also provided a copy of the hard drive to [Rudy Giuliani's attorney](https://www.delawareonline.com/story/news/2020/10/14/meet-wilmington-repairman-who-reportedly-gave-biden-laptop-giuliani-associate/3655753001/) before turning the device over to the FBI. Although no public court records or official FBI confirmations of this possession existed before the claim date, the underlying fact of FBI custody is well-established. The claim does contain a minor inaccuracy: Joe Biden was not the sitting president on October 22, 2020 — [Donald Trump was](https://nypost.com/2020/10/14/), and Biden was only the Democratic presidential nominee at the time, not inaugurated until January 20, 2021 — but this does not undermine the substantive claim about the FBI's possession of the laptop.
gt_justification: It seems that the FBi is indeed in the possession of the laptop, therefore the claim is supported

claim: India’s imports from China increased by 27% in April-August 2020
justification: The claim is supported. Multiple Q&A sources consistently confirm that India's imports from China rose by 27% during April–August 2020 compared to the same period in 2019, based on official Ministry of Commerce data, which typically reports trade values in USD. The figure was available by the claim date of October 22, 2020, as the April–August period had already concluded.
