Key corroborating sources include the [USDA FAS data page](https://fas.usda.gov/data/created) and the [Indian Ministry of Commerce trade statistics document](https://commerce.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/MOC_636977682649387207_LS-03-07-2019.pdf), which confirm both the percentage increase and the official nature of the underlying data.
gt_justification: Q&A 2 and 3 both show that there was a  decrease in the imports from China of 27.63%  between April- August 2020  no an increase as claimed.

claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.
justification: On October 21, 2020, the 7-day rolling average of U.S. COVID-19 deaths was indeed stable at approximately 700–800 per day, and multiple sources characterize the trend as having "plateaued" following the spring 2020 surge ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/coronavirus-in-wisconsin-covid-19-death-toll-hits-400-total-cases-top-10k/), [BMC Medicine](https://bmcmedicine.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12916-020-01791-8), [White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/)), directly supporting the assertion that deaths were "pretty flat" on that date. While broader context—notably rising cases, the typical lag between case and death increases, and the looming "third wave" that drove deaths sharply higher in November and December 2020 ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/in-depth/graphics/2020/03/10/us-coronavirus-map-tracking-united-states-outbreak/4945223002/))—suggests this plateau was temporary, the claim as stated about the current state of deaths on October 21, 2020, is consistent with the available evidence.
gt_justification: The answer and credible source show that the amount of deaths increased so the claim is refuted.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
justification: The fact-check yielded no substantive findings because the Record contains no documented evidence, Q&A analysis, or priorjudgement to evaluate the claim that previous flu vaccines may have made President Trump susceptible to COVID-19. Without any retrieved sources, expert input, or contextual information—including scientific literature on influenza vaccination's potential effect on SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility, details of President Trump's vaccination history and COVID-19 timeline, or the basis of the original article by [Miriam Fauzia](https://www.newsweek.com/)—there is insufficient information to support or refute the claim. Consequently, the verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification: Studys show the flu vaccine does not affect how susceptible some one is to covid-19 so based on this it would mean Donald Trump was not more susceptible.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
justification: The claim contains a significant factual error: Nate McMurray served as Town Supervisor of Grand Island, **New York**, not Nebraska as stated by the claim author ([Spectrum News](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/buffalo/politics/2018/01/10/nate-mcmurray-to-announce-candidacy-for-congress)). While a Grand Island does exist in Nebraska ([Visit Grand Island](https://visitgrandisland.com/plan-a-trip/things-to-do/nature-wildlife.html)), it is a separate and unrelated municipality. Regarding the tax vote assertion, evidence confirms that during McMurray's tenure, the Grand Island Town Board approved budgets that raised taxes—notably the 2020 budget, which increased the overall property tax levy by 3.47%, the general fund tax rate by 2.2%, and the water district tax rate by 34% ([Buffalo News via Wayback Machine](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html)). However, the available sources do not specifically document McMurray's individual vote (yea or nay) on these measures, only attributing approval to "the Town Board" generally, and meeting minutes show the motions to adopt the budget were made by other council members ([ecode360](https://ecode360.com/documents/GR0053/public/466406368.pdf)). The claim is therefore misleading: the incorrect state misrepresents where McMurray served, and the specific assertion that he personally "voted to raise taxes" is not directly substantiated by the evidence, even though tax increases did occur during his tenure.
gt_justification: Confirmed in QA Pairs with Vote date and the vote he cast.

claim: Russia sent medical aid to the US, in the form of medical equipment to help coronavirus patients.
justification: The evidence from multiple sources confirms that Russia did send medical aid to the United States in the form of medical equipment to help coronavirus patients. A Russian military transport plane delivered 60 tons of supplies—including ventilators, masks, and respirators—to JFK airport in New York, accepted by the Trump administration following a phone call between Trump and Putin ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/russian-plane-coronavirus-medical-gear-lands-u-s-after-trump-n1174436)). Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov publicly confirmed the aid ([Anadolu Agency](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/health/russia-sends-medical-aid-to-us-to-help-fight-covid-19/1788290)). However, the shipment actually occurred in late March/early April 2020, not October 2020 as the claim's date suggests. The Russian-made ventilators were later returned after identical models caused fatal fires in Russian hospitals ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/05/21/860143691/u-s-sends-ventilators-to-russia-in-5-6-million-coronavirus-aid-package)), and Russia billed the US approximately $660,000 for the shipment ([ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/russia-bills-us-660k-aid-included-gas-masks/story?id=70451912)). Despite the date discrepancy, the core factual content of the claim is well-supported by evidence.
gt_justification: Evidence finds that Russia did send medical equipment to the United States; however, the U.S. State Department clarified in a press release that the shipment was a "purchase." Evidence also finds that Aventa-M ventilators from Russia were never used by any American hospital, but in October, it was finally discovered where those ventilators ended up—in the trash heap. Hence, a conflicting/cherry-picking claim.

claim: There is a scam involving Santander customers being sent fake bank cards.
justification: The fact-check found no evidence confirming or refuting the specific claim about a scam involving fake Santander bank cards being sent to customers. Searches uncovered various unrelated Santander frauds, including [smishing scams using number spoofing](https://www.thesun.co.uk/money/5805668/santander-warns-customers-about-new-text-message-scam-which-could-hand-your-bank-details-to-criminals/), [authorized push payment (APP) fraud](https://www.santander.co.uk/about-santander/media-centre/press-releases/santander-launches-new-payment-process-to-combat-the-rise-in-payment-scams), [ATM fraud with preloaded debit cards in New York](https://www.ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/news/2020/08/19/santander-bank-glitch-leads-to-atm-fraud), and a [2017 ATM skimming incident in Massachusetts](https://www.doj.nh.gov/consumer/security-breaches/documents/santander-20170619.pdf), but none documented physical fake bank cards being mailed to customers. The absence of matching evidence means the claim cannot be verified or debunked based on available information.
gt_justification: Q&A 1 says that Santander was issuing new bank cards but makes no reference to the claim about a scam being linked to fake issued bank cards,  Q&A 2 and 3 give no answer for their questions so needs more evidence overall for the claim points.

claim: UK Employees unable to work in tier 3 areas will get a combination of Job Support Scheme and Universal Credit, which will mean they get 80% of their wages.
justification: The claim is misleading because it presents the 80% figure as universal when it applies only to a subset of low-income workers. The Job Support Scheme itself only covered 67% of normal salary(capped at £2,100/month) and was not even operational on October 21, 2020 — it launched on November 1, 2020 ([JSS factsheet](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5f8074fb8fa8f50454ce9339/20201009_JSSC_Factsheet_FINAL_EG_1516_002_.pdf)). While Universal Credit could top up the JSS payment to at least 80% for some workers, eligibility depended on income, savings, and dependents — workers with £16,000 in savings would not qualify for any Universal Credit at all, and the Institute for Fiscal Studies calculated that a single person earning £11,000/year with no children would receive only 73% of their usual income, as confirmed by the [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/54633147). The DWP's confirmation of the 80% figure was explicitly limited to low-income workers receiving the full UC entitlement, meaning the claim cherry-picks the most favorable scenario while omitting crucial context about caps, savings thresholds, and the scheme's not-yet-active status.
gt_justification: Rather than the 80% mentioned in the claim, employees will earn 77% according to the sources provided

claim: The large image of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris logo projected onto a Harley-Davidson location in Milwaukee US indicates the motorcycle manufacturer's endorsement of the US Democratic presidential nominee.
justification: No evidence was retrieved, no sources were consulted, and no Q&A analysis was conducted in this fact-check. The Record contains only the claim itself — that a projected Biden-Harris logo on a Harley-Davidson location in Milwaukee constituted a corporate endorsement — without any verification of the image, its origin, or any official statement from Harley-Davidson. Without supporting or contradicting evidence, there is insufficient information to determine the truthfulness of the claim.
gt_justification: The question-answer pair show that the claim is not true.

claim: Scientific American magazine warned that 5G technology is not safe.
justification: The claim is misleading through cherry-picking: while Scientific American did publish Joel Moskowitz's October 2019 opinion piece titled ["We Have No Reason to Believe 5G Is Safe"](https://www.saferemr.com/2020/02/will-scientific-american-clear-up.html), the magazine simultaneously published opposing opinion pieces—Kenneth Foster's ["5G Is Coming: How Worried Should We Be about the Health Risks?"](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/scientific-american-created-confusion-5gs-safety-clear-joel-moskowitz) and David Robert Grimes' ["Don't Fall Prey to Scaremongering about 5G"](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/scientific-american-created-confusion-5gs-safety-clear-joel-moskowitz)—and never issued an official editorial warning against 5G, instead adopting a stance of balance and acknowledging scientific uncertainty. The [naturalnews.com article](https://www.naturalnews.com/2020-10-20-scientific-american-issues-warnings-dangers-of-5g.html) by Cassie B, published on a source rated as a [questionable and discredited outlet](https://mediabiasfactcheck.com/natural-news/) that "routinely publishes false information," misrepresented a single author's opinion as the magazine's institutional position, a framing echoed but not corrected by the [ACSH analysis](https://www.acsh.org/news/2019/10/21/scientific-american-says-5g-dangerous-vegetables-are-junk-food-14351). The claim is therefore technically true on a narrow reading but deeply misleading in its implication, omitting the contradictory context that fundamentally changes the impression conveyed.
gt_justification: There is no convincing evidence that 5G technology is unsafe.

claim: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
justification: The fact-check record reveals contradictory evidence, but the most directly relevant sources support the claim. Sources that denied the incident (e.g., a [Freedom House methodology page](https://freedomhouse.org/reports/freedom-world/freedom-world-research-methodology/created) and an [ABC News story about a Philadelphia bus incident](https://abcnews.go.com/US/philadelphia-police-drag-man-mask-off-public-bus/story?id=70104383/created)) appear tangentially related and do not address the specific incident. In contrast, sources directly relevant to the claim—including a [ClickOrlando article](https://www.clickorlando.com/news/florida/2020/10/20/florida-officer-to-be-disciplined-after-wearing-trump-mask-while-voting/) and a [Florida Politics report](https://floridapolitics.com/archives/375944-miami-officer-uniform-mask/)—confirm that the incident occurred in Miami, Florida, at the Government Center, and that the officer's employer announced disciplinary action. Based on the weight of relevant evidence, the claim is **supported**.
gt_justification: The Q&A pair confirm that the officer in the claim did breach protocol and so you would expect a disciplinary action as the claim states.

claim: Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump are banned from ever operating a charity again because they stole donations for children with cancer.
justification: The claim is largely false and misleading. While Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump were indeed barred fromserving on charities in New York state as part of a [November 2019 settlement](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/judge-orders-trump-pay-2-million-misusing-his-foundation-n1078306) with the New York Attorney General's office, the ban applies only to New York charities—not a blanket lifetime ban on "ever operating a charity" as the claim states. More critically, the claim fabricates the reason for the ban: there is no evidence that donations for children with cancer were stolen. According to the [legal proceedings](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2018/06/15/business/new-york-sues-trump-charity-self-dealing/), the actual misconduct involved the [Trump Foundation](https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/new-york-attorney-general-sues-trump-foundation/) engaging in "repeated and willful self-dealing," misusing funds for personal expenses (portraits, sports memorabilia), settling personal legal disputes, and making an impermissible $25,000 political donation to Florida AG Pam Bondi—not the theft of cancer charity donations as alleged.
gt_justification:
The court order did not ban Trump, Trump and Trump from operating a charity. If they had been the mandatory training would be irrelevant and pointless.
There is no evidence that the misused funds were ring-fenced for or allocated to supporting children with cancer.

claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
justification: The claim is refuted because it mischaracterizes how the ACA's individual mandate penalty worked. The $10,000 figure was a maximum cap (equal to the national average bronze plan premium), not a standard penalty applied to everyone; the penalty was actually calculated as the greater of a flat dollar amount (~$695 per adult) or 2.5% of household income above tax filing thresholds, meaning lower-income individuals who "couldn't afford" coverage would face penalties far below $10,000, if any ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-reform/issue-brief/how-many-of-the-uninsured-can-purchase-a-marketplace-plan-for-less-than-their-shared-responsibility-penalty/)). Furthermore, the ACA included hardship and affordability exemptions to protect people who genuinely could not afford coverage, and provided premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies to help lower-income individuals afford insurance ([CBPP](https://www.cbpp.org/research/health/improving-aca-subsidies-for-low-and-moderate-income-consumers-is-key-to-increasing)). Most critically, the federal individual mandate penalty was reduced to $0 effective January 1, 2019—over a year before the claim was made on October 20, 2020—through the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 ([Holland & Hart](https://www.hollandhart.com/2019-repeal-of-the-affordable-care-acts-individual-mandate-penalties)), making the claim factually impossible at the time it was posted.
gt_justification: The 2nd Q&A pair point out that from 2019 there was no more penalty for having no health insurance in the US, whilst the claim was made in 2020.

claim: Hunter Biden was chairman of the Nobel Peace Prize winning World Food Program.
justification: The claim is refuted because Hunter Biden served as **Board Chairman of World Food Program USA**—a separate U.S.-based nonprofit that supports the UN World Food Programme—not as chairman of the actual UN World Food Programme (WFP), which is the entity that won the [Nobel Peace Prize in 2020](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/world-food-program-wins-nobel-peace-prize). Multiple sources confirm this distinction, including [Hunter Biden's own lawyer George Mesires](https://medium.com/@george.mesires/a-statement-on-behalf-of-hunter-biden-dated-october-13-2019-d80bc11087ab) and reporting on [his role at World Food Program USA's Annual McGovern-Dole Leadership Award Ceremony](https://sanantonioreport.org/before-hunter-biden-there-was-billy-carter-neil-bush-and-others/world-food-program-usas-annual-mcgovern-dole-leadership-award-ceremony/), where his title is consistently listed as "World Food Program USA Board Chairman." The claim falsely conflates these two distinct organizations to imply he chaired the Nobel Peace Prize–winning UN agency itself.
gt_justification: Hunter Biden served as chairman from 2011 to 2015, according to the nonprofit’s annual reports.

claim: National Testing Agency (NTA) has made a major blunder in NEET Exam Result 2020. They stated that the all India topper had failed.
justification: The fact-check confirms that NTA did make an error in the NEET 2020 results: Mridul Rawat was initially declared as failed with 329/720 on the first marksheet, but after rechecking, his score was corrected to 650/720, revealing him as the All India Topper in the **Scheduled Tribe (ST) category** ([Livemint](https://www.livemint.com/education/news/neet-2020-failed-candidate-turns-out-to-be-all-india-topper-in-st-category-11603182789566.html), [India.com](https://www.india.com/education/neet-2020-result-blunder-aspirant-declared-failed-emerges-as-topper-deets-here-4179014/)). However, the overall All India toppers were Soyeb Aftab and Akanksha Singh, who both scored a perfect 720/720 and were never declared as failed ([OneIndia](https://www.oneindia.com/india/neet-2020-when-a-topper-was-declared-failed-3165796.html)). The claim is therefore misleading because it conflates the ST category topper with the overall all-India topper, omitting the crucial contextual distinction and creating a significantly different impression of the incident, warranting a **cherry-picking** verdict.
gt_justification: Q&A source information proves that this claim is false. India's National Testing Agency advised via a press release that the social media claims were not true and were to be disregarded.

claim: Joe Biden said 'If Your 8-Year-Old Child Says They Want To Be Transgender, They Have A Right To Transition'.
justification: The claim that Joe Biden said "If Your 8-Year-Old Child Says They Want To Be Transgender, They Have A Right To Transition" is **refuted** by the evidence. While Biden did address the topic of transgender children during the [ABC News Town Hall on October 15, 2020](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/biden-town-hall-transgender-rights-zero-discrimination/), his actual words were substantively different: "The idea that an eight-year-old child or a 10-year-old child decides you know, I decided I want to be transgender. That's what I think I'd like to be. It'd make my life a lot easier. There should be zero discrimination." Multiple sources, including [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/biden-town-hall-transgender-rights-zero-discrimination/) and [The Federalist](https://thefederalist.com/2020/10/19/joe-biden-tells-mom-he-supports-transgendering-eight-year-old-kids/), confirm this actual quote, and none corroborate the exact wording in the claim. Biden's real statement focused on "zero discrimination" rather than asserting a "right to transition," and the claim's attributed quote distorts both the content and nuance of his remarks. The claim, originating from [Pastor Greg Locke](https://www.tennessean.com/story/news/2016/05/01/target-blasting-pastor-greg-locke-channels-anger-new-way/83615088/)—a source with no journalistic credentials—presents a fabricated direct quote.
gt_justification: There is not enough evidence to support or refute the claim

claim: White House coronavirus adviser Dr. Anthony Fauci wrote a 2008 paper that found most 1918-1919 Spanish Influenza pandemic deaths were because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Dr. Anthony Fauci did co-author a 2008 paper — "Predominant Role of Bacterial Pneumonia as a Cause of Death in Pandemic Influenza" (Morens, Taubenberger, and Fauci, [*Journal of Infectious Diseases*](https://medlineplus.gov/download/genetics/condition/pyle-disease.pdf/created)) — which concluded that the majority of 1918–1919 pandemic deaths resulted from secondary bacterial pneumonia rather than the influenza virus itself. However, the claim's critical assertion that these deaths were caused by mask-wearing is entirely unsupported: the paper never discussed masks as a causal factor, instead attributing bacterial superinfections (from pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus aureus*) to influenza-induced damage of the respiratory tract ([PAHO](https://www3.paho.org/english/dd/pin/Number18_article5.htm/created)). Multiple sources, including the paper's actual findings and subsequent medical analyses ([ERJ](https://erj.ersjournals.com/content/56/4/2001727/created)), consistently confirm that the mask-wearing link is a misrepresentation of the paper's conclusions, making the claim false.
gt_justification: There is no mention in the 2008 paper wearing masks could be responsible for the secondary bacterial pneumonia. respiratory–tract bacteria.

claim: Dr Anthony Fauci wrote a paper regarding the Spanish Flu and stated that the majority of deaths in 1918-1919 was because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: Dr. Anthony Fauci did co-author a 2008 paper on the 1918–1919 Spanish Flu pandemic (titled "Predominant Role of Bacterial Pneumonia as a Cause of Death in Pandemic Influenza," co-authored with David M. Morens and Jeffery K. Taubenberger), which indeed concluded that the majority of deaths were due to secondary bacterial pneumonia infections ([HHS source](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/For%20Posting_Hauguel_NIAID%20Universal%20Influenza%20Vaccine%20Portfolio_16x9_Remediated%20%28002%29.pdf/created), [PBS NewsHour](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/analysis-why-some-schools-stayed-open-during-the-1918-flu-pandemic/created)). However, the paper attributed these deaths to bacterial co-infections following the influenza virus—exacerbated by the lack of antibiotics—not to mask-wearing ([History.com](https://www.history.com/news/1918-pandemic-public-health-campaigns/created)). The claim falsely conflates the paper's legitimate finding about bacterial pneumonia with a fabricated assertion that masks caused these deaths, a misrepresentation that has been widely debunked.
gt_justification: No link to masks was mentioned.

claim: India's imports from China increased by 27% during the period April-August 2020.
justification: Multiple independent sources consistently confirm the 27% increase in India's imports from China during April–August 2020. The [Bank for International Settlements](https://www.bis.org/publ/bppdf/bispap83.pdf/created) reports that imports totaled $33.52 billion during that period, a 27% rise over the same period in 2019 (approximately $26.39 billion). [Oxfam](https://www.oxfam.org/en/india-extreme-inequality-numbers/created), citing official data, corroborates the 27% figure, and a [USITC](https://www.usitc.gov/home/created) source explicitly states that "India's imports from China rose exactly 27% in April-August" 2020. The figure refers to monetary value (USD), which is standard for official trade statistics. The claim is well-supported across these independent sources.
gt_justification: the imports declined during this period

claim: The daughter of Muahammadu Buhari (the President of Nigeria) is a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC).
justification: Multiple sources confirm that Muhammadu Buhari was serving as President of Nigeria on October 19, 2020 (having been reelected in February 2019), and that his daughter [Zahra Buhari](https://cs.wellesley.edu/~pmetaxas/Research/Information_Credibility_on_Twitter.pdf/created) was appointed as a non-executive director on the [NNPC board](https://uniosun.edu.ng/index.php/itemlist/category/169-profile.html?start=110/created) as of that date, with the appointment documented in the Federal Government Gazette. Buhari has multiple daughters, but Zahra is the one specifically identified as an NNPC board member. While no official government or NNPC press announcement was found, and the exact appointment date and length of service are unspecified, the available evidence directly and clearly supports the claim.
gt_justification: Q&As find that Muhammedu Buhari's (the President of Nigeria's) unnamed daughter is not a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC).

claim: Chinese Diplomats Assault Taiwan Counterparts in Fiji
justification: The claim is well-supported by multiple corroborating sources. On October 8, 2020, two Chinese embassy workers gatecrashed a Taiwan National Day celebration at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, Fiji, and physically assaulted a Taiwanese official, who sustained a head wound requiring hospital treatment. Taiwan's foreign ministry officially condemned the incident as "the first ever physical confrontation between members of Beijing and Taipei's diplomatic missions," and [Fiji police launched an investigation](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20201019-taiwan-says-chinese-diplomats-assaulted-official-in-fiji). The [Chinese Embassy in Fiji](http://fj.china-embassy.gov.cn/eng/sgxw/202010/t20201019_881183.htm) offered a competing account alleging the Taiwanese side initiated the violence, but this represents a conflicting narrative rather than a refutation of the core claim. The incident received widespread international media coverage, including by [France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20201019-taiwan-says-chinese-diplomats-assaulted-official-in-fiji) and [The Guardian](https://www.grubsheet.com.au/grubsheet-story-goes-global/), confirming the event's occurrence and the essential details of the claim.
gt_justification: It seems both attacked each other based on the QA pairs.

claim: The Iowa Farm Bureau, US says that it would no longer be endorsing US Republican Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst for her re-election
justification: The fact-check confirms that the Iowa Farm Bureau Federation — a legitimate U.S. organization founded in 1918 and described as "Iowa's largest grassroots farm organization" ([iowafarmbureau.com](https://www.iowafarmbureau.com/WebsitePageFile/File/F0EFA6AD-6457-4F15-B236-22D9949E78DD/Cenntenial_Web.pdf)) — did withdraw its endorsement of Republican Iowa Senator Joni Ernst in October 2020, as referenced in multiple sources including [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/nebraska-man-accused-making-threats-ernst-n780866/) and [ACLED data](https://acleddata.com/2020/09/03/demonstrations-political-violence-in-america-new-data-for-summer-2020/). The withdrawal pertained to her 2020 re-election campaign, and Ernst was indeed a Republican senator from Iowa seeking re-election that year ([Des Moines Register](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/opinion/columnists/2019/02/28/joni-ernst-defy-history-re-elected-2020-grassley-harkin-trump-senate-politics-elections-republicans/3016068002/)). The timing aligns with the claim date of October 18, 2020, and the act of withdrawing inherently confirms a prior endorsement existed. No specific reason for the withdrawal was identified, but this does not undermine the core factual claim, which is consistently supported across sources.
gt_justification: From the 3rd question and answer pair it seems the the Iowa Farm Bureau is still endorsing republican senator joni ernst. Therefore the cliam is refuted

claim: Joe and Jill Biden's income has increased recently.
justification: The tax return data for Joe and Jill Biden shows a clear declining income trend in the years leading up to October 2020, directly contradicting the claim that their income had "increased recently." They reported approximately $11 million in adjusted gross income in 2017, more than $4.5 million in 2018, and about $985,000 in 2019—representing a consistent year-over-year decrease ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/biden-releases-2019-tax-returns-ahead-first-debate-n1241387), [CPA Practice Advisor](https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2020/09/30/biden-2019-tax-returns-show-high-income-and-high-tax-rate/40527/)). While their post-White House earnings were substantially higher than their government salary, this comparison reflects the period after leaving the vice presidency in early 2017, not a "recent" increase as of the claim's date. The documented year-over-year decline from 2017 through 2019 definitively refutes the assertion.
gt_justification: The answers show that the couples income in recent years had increased so it is supported.

claim: Hunter Biden (son of US president Joe Biden)  had 25,000 pics of him torturing and raping children under 10 in China on his laptop.
justification: Multiple elements of the claim are demonstrably false. Joe Biden was not the sitting US President on October 18, 2020—he was a presidential candidate who didn't assume office until January 20, 2021 ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/archive/articles/2020/october)). While a laptop associated with Hunter Biden did surface in October 2020 reportedly containing "nearly 25,000 images," these were described by the [New York Post](https://nypost.com/2020/10/16/hunter-biden-emails-pics-reveal-wild-life-pained-soul/) as "sexually explicit selfies and porn" along with personal photos—not images of torture or rape of children. No forensic examination, credible news organization, or independent expert confirmed the existence of images depicting Hunter Biden torturing or raping children under 10 in China; [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/hunter-biden-laptop-new-york-post-story/) explicitly stated it "has not seen or corroborated the data supposedly on the hard drive," and references to child pornography came only from unverified secondhand claims via partisan outlets like [OAN and National File](https://nationalfile.com/bombshell-ny-post-refuses-to-publish-all-25000-hunter-pics-after-reports-they-include-child-porn/). Furthermore, the [Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8842709/Joe-Bidens-son-crack-pipe-new-low-dirtiest-election-writes-TOM-LEONARD.html) reporting on the laptop contents makes no mention of child exploitation material of any kind, and Hunter Biden has never been charged, arrested, or convicted of any crime involving child sexual abuse material ([Radar Online](https://radaronline.com/t/hunter-biden/?page=5)).
gt_justification: Answers do not confirm or deny this.

claim: A third of excess deaths in the United States between 1 March and  1 August 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic could not be directly attributed to the coronavirus
justification: **Summary:** Thefact-check record contains no documented evidence, retrieved sources, or prior Q&A analysis to evaluate the Claim. Without any underlying data—such as the cited study's methodology, the specific figures for total excess deaths versus those directly attributed to COVID-19 during March–August 2020, or corroborating analyses from independent sources—no factual basis exists to confirm, refute, or contextualize the statistic presented by the [Washington Examiner article](https://web.archive.org/web/20210310055253/https://archive.is/EKPAJ). Consequently, the verdict remains **"not enough information."**
gt_justification: From the last answer it seems that the excess death was indeed 1 third. Therefore the claim is supported

claim: Prominent US Democrat party members including Hillary and Bill Clinton, were running a child sex-trafficking ring in the basement of a Washington, D.C., pizzeria.
justification: The claim, known as the "Pizzagate" conspiracy theory, is definitively false. While Comet Ping Pong does have a basement, it was used for pizza preparation and storage — not trafficking — and both the [FBI and D.C. Metropolitan Police](https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/local/dc-pizzeria-owner-receiving-death-threats-after-conspiracy-theory-circulates/89424/) found no evidence of any child sex-trafficking ring; neither Hillary nor Bill Clinton was ever charged, arrested, or convicted in connection with such allegations. The theory originated from [4chan users misinterpreting "cheese pizza" (slang for child pornography) in John Podesta's leaked emails](https://rationalwiki.org/wiki/Pizzagate), and the purported "evidence" consists entirely of [speculative interpretations of art, social media posts, and coded language](https://michaelmhughes.medium.com/refuting-pizzagate-the-conspiracy-that-wasnt-6ae01001aa5e) — no documents, witness testimony, or corroborating victims have ever surfaced. [PolitiFact rated the claim "pants on fire!"](https://www.pmq.com/the-lessons-of-pizzagate/) The only real-world consequence was the [December 2016 armed incident in which Edgar Welch stormed the restaurant, found nothing, and was arrested](https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/local/man-with-assault-rifle-arrested-at-comet-ping-pong-in-nw-dc/111295/).
gt_justification: The sources show that this claim is incorrect and is false news so the claim is refuted.

claim: Anthony Weiner’s laptop contained proof Hillary Clinton & her associates are involved in child trafficking & paedophilia
justification: The fact-check confirms that Anthony Weiner's laptop was indeed seized by the FBI in 2016, but as part of an investigation into Weiner's own illicit communications with a minor, not Clinton. The laptop's relevant contents were thousands of emails between Huma Abedin and Hillary Clinton related to the private email server investigation, which led FBI Director James Comey to notify Congress of the reopened probe—no evidence of child trafficking or paedophilia involving Clinton or her associates was ever found. No court, law enforcement agency, or judicial body has ever determined that Clinton or her associates were involved in such crimes, and reputable fact-checking organizations including [PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com), [Snopes](https://www.snopes.com), [FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org), [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com), and the [Associated Press](https://www.ap.org) have thoroughly debunked the assertion as a well-known QAnon-associated conspiracy theory with no credible substantiation.
gt_justification: The FBI cleared Hilary Clinton of the charges

claim: “Red-tagging” is a term invented by the Communist Party of the Philippines, the New People's Army, and the National Democratic Front (CPP-NPA-NDF).
justification: Multiple independent and credible sources consistently attribute the coinage of "red-tagging" to the CPP-NPA-NDF. [IFEX](https://ifex.org/how-red-baiting-undermines-truth-telling-in-the-philippines/) and [Rappler](https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/fact-check/261107-photo-former-nujp-chair-connects-cpp-npa-ndf) both state the term "was coined by the CPP-NPA-NDF as propaganda to discredit government security operations," while a [U.S. government report](https://www.trade.gov/us-export-controls) adds that "no credible evidence shows 'red-tagging' in Philippine sources before CPP-NPA-NDF propagandists introduced it in the early 2000s." No source identifies an earlier origin, an alternative inventor, or provides contradicting evidence. While no direct, self-attributed statement from the CPP-NPA-NDF explicitly claiming invention was found, the consistent attribution across multiple independent sources and the documented absence of any prior use in Philippine discourse collectively support the claim.
gt_justification:
“Red-tagging” has been in existence before  CPP-NPA-NDF were founded. 

The word ''Red-tagging'' was used in a US document dating back to 1947. And the CPP-NPA-NDF were founded in December 26, 1968.

claim: NBC News Kristen Welker gave thousands of dollars to Obama, Clinton and Biden, is registered as a Democrat & her family spent Christmas with the Obamas at the White House.
justification: The claim misattributes political donations to NBC News journalist Kristen Welker personally, when in fact the donations to Obama (~$20,000), Clinton ($2,100), and Biden ($3,300) were made by her parents, Julie and Harvey Welker, according to the [NY Post](https://nypost.com/2020/10/17/kristen-welker-next-debate-moderator-has-deep-democrat-ties/). While Welker was registered as a Democrat in Washington, DC in 2012 and Rhode Island in 2004, her current voter registration status is unconfirmed, making the claim that she "is registered as a Democrat" unsupported. The assertion that her family spent Christmas with the Obamas at the White House is accurate, as they did celebrate Christmas there in 2012. The claim thus mixes verifiable facts (the Christmas visit, past Democratic registration, and family donations) with a misleading attribution of those donations directly to Welker herself, creating a distorted impression of her political activity.
gt_justification:
Q2 shows that the person named in the claim did donate money to the people named in the claim, but at lesser amounts than claimed.
Q&A 3  states the person named in the claim did also visit the white hose at christmas as claimed, but also says she attended with other guests and may have been there in a professional manner not a personal one. so some facts are similar to as claimed, whilst others are taken out of context.

claim: In the US lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 which were observed in 2020.
justification: The claim that US lockdowns are "partly responsible" for non-COVID-19 excess deaths in 2020 is not directly supported nor refuted by the available evidence. The CDC confirmed that approximately one-third of excess deaths from January through October 2020 were not attributed to COVID-19, with leading causes including heart disease, Alzheimer disease/dementia, and diabetes ([CDC MMWR](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/pdfs/mm6942e2-H.pdf)), and acknowledged these deaths may be "indirectly related to the pandemic (e.g., because of disruptions in health care access or utilization)" or misclassified COVID-19 deaths. However, no source reviewed isolates or quantifies lockdowns as a distinct causal factor separate from broader pandemic effects. Instead, non-COVID-19 excess deaths are attributed to general pandemic-related factors such as fear of seeking medical care ([Penn Today](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/US-covid-deaths-may-be-underestimated-36-percent)), economic and mental health impacts, and healthcare disruptions. Additionally, a [PLOS ONE study](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0261759) defined US lockdown measures but did not link them to non-COVID-19 excess mortality. The CDC has not explicitly attributed any portion of non-COVID-19 excess deaths to lockdown policies, and the claim's specific causal assertion lacks direct evidentiary support in the reviewed sources.
gt_justification: The Q&A's only mention excess death due to covid and so no data for other causes such as the claimed 'lockdowns' so more evidence is needed.

claim: Pennsylvania US rejects 372,000 mail-in ballots.
justification: The 372,000 figure originates from a [ProPublica/Philadelphia Inquirer investigation](https://www.propublica.org/article/pennsylvanias-rejection-of-372-000-ballot-applications-bewilders-voters-and-strains-election-staff) and is factually accurate, but the claim materially misrepresents what it represents: these were rejected ballot **applications** (requests), not rejected mail-in ballots themselves. Over 90% of the rejections—approximately 336,000—were duplicate applications from voters who had unknowingly checked a box to receive ballots for both the primary and general election, and [those voters could still receive a ballot or vote in person on Election Day](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/pennsylvania-mail-ballot-rejections-duplicate-applications-20201016.html), meaning no voters were ultimately disenfranchised. The headline's omission of this critical context—particularly that these were applications rather than ballots, and that the vast majority were harmless duplicates—creates a significantly more alarming impression than what actually occurred, making this a case of cherry-picking and misleading framing.
gt_justification: It was applications that were rejected and not actual ballots.

claim: It's unclear how Joe Biden acquired his recent wealth since leaving office in 2017
justification: The claim that "it's unclear how Joe Biden acquired his recent wealth since leaving office in 2017" is contradicted by extensive public documentation. Reputable sources such as [Voice of America](https://www.voanews.com/a/usa_us-politics_biden-and-wife-made-more-15m-after-leaving-office/6171514.html) and the [Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/news/politics/2019/07/09/biden-earned-millions-after-leaving-white-house-financial-disclosures-show/YDpLcGshpG7pJNzrTTRgWO/story.html) have reported in detail that Biden and his wife earned more than $15 million in the two years after leaving the Vice Presidency, with identifiable income from book deals (including his 2017 memoir "Promise Me, Dad"), a professorship at the University of Pennsylvania, six-figure speaking fees, and a federal pension. These income sources are further verified by publicly accessible tax returns for 2017–2019 and OGE Form 278e financial disclosures available through [disclosures.org](http://www.disclosures.org/joe-biden-financial-disclosures/), directly refuting the claim's assertion of uncertainty.
gt_justification: He made $15.6 million in the 2 years after he left office mostly through speaking fees

claim: India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani installed Jinnah's portrait at AMU.
justification: There is no documented evidence in the Record to evaluate whether India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani installed Jinnah's portrait at AMU. No initial Q&A, retrieved sources, or prior analysis were recorded, leaving key questions entirely unaddressed — including Usmani's party affiliation, whether he placed a portrait of Jinnah, and the circumstances or authenticity of the alleged event. Without any supporting or refuting evidence, a factual determination cannot be made, and the claim remains unverified.
gt_justification: The portrait of Jinnah has been on display at AMU since 1938, so India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani could not have installed it. Hence, the claim is refuted.

claim: Donald Trump Jr. said, “My father doesn’t need to rape women. It’s more likely a woman would rape him. That’s how popular he is.”
justification: The fact-check examined whether Donald Trump Jr. made the specific quoted statement attributed to him, searching multiple sources for verification. Two key sources were reviewed: a [BuzzFeed article](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/tasneemnashrulla/donald-trump-jr-said-this-rape-apologist-deserves-a-pultizer) documenting a Twitter exchange involving Trump Jr. and Mike Cernovich, and a [Vox article](https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2016/10/13/13274632/donald-trump-jr-sexual-assault) covering his 2016 defense of his father on Charlotte radio station WBT following the Access Hollywood tape and allegations from multiple women. While both sources confirm that Trump Jr. defended his father against sexual misconduct allegations in various contexts, **none of the examined sources contain the exact quote** in question. No information was found about what Trump Jr. said on the claim date of October 16, 2020, leaving the attribution unverified. Based on the available evidence, the claim remains unsubstantiated.
gt_justification: no reliable source has been provided.

claim: Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) is delivering 1kg bleaching powder, chlorine tablets to people’s doorsteps
justification: The fact-check could not verify or refute the claim because no evidence was found regarding HMWSSB's specific doorstep delivery program for bleaching powder and chlorine tablets around October 2020. The only information gathered addressed the general purpose of these products—disinfecting drinking water and eliminating waterborne diseases—based on a generic government publication on chemical industries ([dcmsme.gov.in](https://www.dcmsme.gov.in/publications/pmryprof/chem/ch9.pdf)). Without an official HMWSSB announcement, press release, news coverage, or denial from that period, there is insufficient information to determine whether the described delivery scheme actually existed, resulting in a verdict of "not enough information."
gt_justification: Seems that chlorine is indeed being handed out. Therefore the claim is supported

claim: A man who received four ballot applications votes four times in the 2020 election.
justification: The fact-check found no confirmation from any official election authority or law enforcement agency regarding the specific incident of a man receiving four ballot applications and voting four times in the 2020 election. The only available evidence ([Fox29](https://www.fox29.com/news/receiving-multiple-ballot-applications-wont-let-you-vote-more-than-once-heres-why)) describes general safeguards against multiple voting—such as voter file checks, unique ID tracking, signature verification, and coding on ballot envelopes—but does not address whether this particular man's four votes were actually cast, counted, or rejected. Without official confirmation, denial, or specific documentation of the alleged incident, there is insufficient evidence to either support or refute the claim.
gt_justification: It seems from the QAs that counting votes twice is illegal. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Most deaths in the 1918 influenza pandemic originated from bacterial pneumonia caused by face masks and that Dr Anthony Fauci, the US government’s top expert in the fight against Covid-19, knew about it.
justification: No evidence was available to evaluate the claim. The fact-check record contained no initial Q&A, no retrieved sources, and no documented findings to assess whether most deaths in the 1918 influenza pandemic were caused by bacterial pneumonia linked to face masks, or whether Dr. Anthony Fauci acknowledged such a link. As stated in the [archived article](https://archive.ph/Z1d7o) where the claim originated by Colleen Huber, the claim itself could not be verified or refuted due to the complete absence of supporting or contradicting evidence in the record. **Verdict: not enough information.**
gt_justification: there is no evidence this happened in 1918, and no evidence that mask wearing causes bacterial pneumonia.

claim: BJP MP Kirron Kher Said "Rape Is A Part Of Indian Culture And It Can't Be Stopped"
justification: Multiple sources, including [Vox](https://www.vox.com/2019/5/2/18522758/facebook-fact-checking-partnership-daily-caller) and [NDTV archives](https://archives.ndtv.com/articles/2018-01.html), confirm that BJP Chandigarh MP Kirron Kher did state "rape is a part of Indian culture and it can't be stopped" during a 2018 media interaction, with Vox explicitly noting the remark was "confirmed by independent audio recordings." While a [Ministry of Women and Child Development handbook](https://wcd.nic.in/sites/default/files/Handbook%20on%20Sexual%20Harassment%20of%20Women%20at%20Workplace.pdf) indicates the statement was "distorted out of context," this does not refute that she actually uttered those words, and she never retracted or clarified the remark. The claim's date of October 15, 2020 is inaccurate—the statement originated in 2018—but the core assertion that Kirron Kher made this statement is supported by the evidence.
gt_justification: The MP has said comments about rape but not the phrase that it can not be stopped. The claim was also on a Facebook page that spreads fake news.

claim: A message will be sent to your phone claiming to show that the Covid19 curve is flattening in India, But It will contain a malicious file
justification: India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a warning in October 2020 about a malicious WhatsApp message falsely claiming to show India's COVID-19 curve flattening, which contained an Android APK disguised as a video exploiting a WhatsApp MP4 vulnerability. This was corroborated by cybersecurity firms [Kaspersky and Quick Heal](https://www.cnn.com/2018/09/30/tech/facebook-whatsapp-india-misinformation/index.html/created), and the [Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre and Ministry of Home Affairs](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2018/06/04/how-americans-have-viewed-government-surveillance-and-privacy-since-snowden-leaks//created) documented multiple infections from this campaign, confirming the claim's details regarding timing, delivery channel, lure, and malicious content.
gt_justification: QA pairs state it is fake.

claim: US Sen Kamala Harris failed the bar exam  (qualifying examination for lawyers)on her first attempt
justification: Multiple sources, including [UC Law SF](https://uclawsf.edu/2016/01/05/new-years-message-from-david-faigman/) and the [California Bar Journal](https://www.calbarjournal.com/June2015/TopHeadlines.aspx/created), confirm that no official record or credible report substantiates the claim that Kamala Harris failed the bar exam on her first attempt. Evidence indicates that Harris took the **District of Columbia** bar exam on her first attempt—not the California bar—and was ultimately admitted to the California bar, passing it in 1990 according to her [official biography via Vault](https://vault.com/blogs/vaults-law-blog-legal-careers-and-industry-news/career-path-of-kamala-harris-from-activist-daughter-to-vp-nominee). While the [LA Times archives](https://web.archive.org/web/20201125172649/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-01-20-mn-10438-story.html) note that California bar pass rates hovered around or below 50% in the 1980s—making first-time failure common—this contextual information does not validate the specific claim about Harris. Major fact-checking organizations have likewise found the claim unsubstantiated, and the available evidence actively indicates it is false.
gt_justification: Answer is supported by the source - that U.S. Sen Kamala Harris did fail her first bar exam.

claim: US Judge Amy Coney Barrett graduated at the top of her law school class at Notre Dame Law School
justification: The fact-check confirms that Amy Coney Barrett graduated from Notre Dame Law School in 1997, finishing first in her class *summa cum laude*, as documented by [Notre Dame Law School](https://law.nd.edu/news-events/news/hamburg-honor-scholars-bucerius-law-school) and corroborated by [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/who-amy-coney-barrett-trump-s-supreme-court-nominee-n1241192) and the [Senate Judiciary Committee](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/rep/releases/chairman-graham-announces-hearing-dates-for-judge-barretts-supreme-court-nomination). As of October 14, 2020, she was serving as a U.S. federal appellate judge on the Seventh Circuit, making "US Judge" an accurate descriptor. While a few retrieved sources (from [collegetransitions.com](https://www.collegetransitions.com/dataverse/top-feeders-law-school), a [Yale bulletin](https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/yale-law-school-2005-2006.pdf), and a [notredame.edu.au page](https://www.notredame.edu.au/about-us/schools/sydney/law)) falsely claimed she transferred and earned her degree elsewhere, these were identified as unreliable or fabricated, contradicting well-established public records. Both components of the claim are therefore supported.
gt_justification: Judge Amy Coney Barrett graduated at the top of her law school class

claim: Saved by the Bell actor, Dustin Diamond died in a prison riot.
justification: Dustin Diamond, the actor known for playing Screech on "Saved by the Bell" ([The Sun](https://www.thesun.co.uk/who/dustin-diamond/)), did not die in a prison riot; he died of stage 4 small cell lung cancer on February 1, 2021, at age 44. While the claim circulated on October 14, 2020, every credible source confirms he was alive at that time and passed away months later from cancer, not blunt force trauma. Diamond was convicted of a misdemeanor (not a felony) in 2019, served a short sentence, and was released well before his death. Sources purporting to confirm a prison riot death—citing institutions like the Wisconsin Department of Corrections, OJP, or Dartmouth—were identified as unreliable, fabricated, or logically inconsistent (e.g., a 1992 newspaper allegedly confirming 2020 events). The claim is false.
gt_justification: According to the answers source information the actor Duston Diamond died at a date later than that quoted in the metadata, and of Stage 4 small cell carcinoma, not in a prison riot.

claim: Controversial abortion methods are allowed under New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020).
justification: The fact-check found that New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act 2020 was indeed passed and permits abortion on request up to 20 weeks, with later abortions allowed subject to qualified health professional assessment ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-51955148), [Simple Wikipedia](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020)). However, regarding the specific claim that "controversial abortion methods" are allowed, the only source making this assertion is Right To Life UK itself—the claim's author—which claims there are "no legal restrictions on controversial methods of abortion such as intact dilation and extraction abortions" ([Right To Life UK](https://righttolife.org.uk/news/nz-pm-rushes-worlds-most-extreme-abortion-law-into-law-while-country-distracted-with-pandemic)). This source does not cite the statutory text, and no independent or neutral legal analysis was retrieved to verify which specific methods are permitted or prohibited under the Act. Given the claim's vagueness about what constitutes "controversial methods" and the absence of independent verification, there is insufficient evidence to confirm or refute the claim definitively.
gt_justification: The answers and credible sources show that they do not have controversial abortion methods so the claim is refuted.

claim: Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Chairman Chito Gascon called a “surprise military attack” by the Philippine Army,  conducted on members of the New People’s Army (NPA) a “violation of human rights.”
justification: The claim is supported by the evidence gathered. Chito Gascon was indeed serving as Chairman of the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) of the Philippines in October 2020 ([Rappler](https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/inside-track/181966-chr-bigger-2018-budget-chito-gascon-resign-pantaleon-alvarez/)), and a military operation around that time involved troops of the 1st Infantry Battalion clashing with alleged NPA members in Sitio Coloconto, Barangay Bulsa, San Juan, Batangas ([PNA](https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1043164)). Gascon characterized the operation as a "surprise military attack" and a "violation of human rights," which aligns with the claim. However, it is worth noting that the NPA membership of those targeted was based solely on military claims without independent verification, which contextualizes Gascon's human rights concerns about the incident.
gt_justification: The answers show that the page is a fake news site so the claim is refuted.

claim: IMAGE CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP CURRENTLY FACES A COURT CASE FOR ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTING A 13-YEAR-OLD
justification: The claim is supported by multiple sources. A woman using the pseudonyms "Katie Johnson" and "Jane Doe" filed a federal lawsuit alleging Donald Trump raped her at age 13 at a Jeffrey Epstein-hosted party in 1994–1995; the case was originally filed in April 2016, voluntarily dismissed in November 2016, and then **refiled in October 2020** in Manhattan federal court, as reported by [Courthouse News](https://www.courthousenews.com/rape-allegations-refiled-against-trump/). [PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2020/jun/03/facebook-posts/no-proof-donald-trump-raped-13-year-old-girl-1994/) verified the image of the court documents as authentic, and Trump's counsel Alan Garten responded to the refiled suit, confirming the case was active against Trump personally at the time. The October 2020 refiling aligns with the claim date of October 14, 2020, making the assertion that Trump "currently faces" such a court case factually accurate.
gt_justification: Answer states trump attended no such court appearance and a case was dropped in 2016 which was similar.

claim: The iPhone 12 won’t come with earphones and a charging adapter.
justification: The claim is fully supported by multiple reliable sources. Apple's official website explicitly stated that "iPhone 12 and iPhone 12 mini do not include a power adapter or EarPods," and [MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2020/10/13/iphone-12-ships-without-earpods-or-charger/) confirmed on October 13, 2020 that the entire iPhone 12 lineup — including the iPhone 12, 12 mini, 12 Pro, and 12 Pro Max — shipped without EarPods or a power adapter, containing only a Lightning to USB-C cable. This marked a deliberate change from the iPhone 11, which had included both items. Apple officially framed the removal as an environmental initiative to reduce e-waste and carbon emissions, with Lisa Jackson, Apple's VP of environment, policy and social initiatives, stating that the decision would "reduce carbon emissions and avoid the mining and use of precious materials" ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/14/apple-praised-for-removing-earpods-and-charger-from-iphone-12-box.html), [Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/sciencetech/article-8840611/Apple-customers-outraged-learning-799-iPhone-12-NOT-include-charger-EarPods.html)).
gt_justification: Evidence shows that Apple has removed the earphones and a charging adapter from Iphone 12 boxes to reduce carbon emissions and cut back on the mining and use of materials used to make these items. Hence, the claim is supported.

claim: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) does not make it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support.
justification: The fact-check record contains no documented evidence, Q&A entries, or findings from any investigationinto the claim regarding New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) and its provisions on medical support for babies born alive after an abortion. Without access to the actual text of the Act, legal analyses, parliamentary debates, or credible sources addressing this specific issue, there is insufficient information to confirm or deny the claim's accuracy. The claim therefore cannot be evaluated based on the available record.
gt_justification: The answer and source show that the claim is not correct so it is refuted.
